prs.title: fix(codex): bind-mount host auth.json so refreshed tokens reach future spawns
prs.body:
## What

Changes `src/providers/codex.ts` to bind-mount the host's `~/.codex/auth.json` directly into each container instead of copying it at spawn time. The per-session codex dir is still mounted (for `config.toml`); the auth.json file mount sits on top of it.

## Why

ChatGPT OAuth uses single-use rotating refresh tokens. With the previous copy-based approach, once any codex session refreshed its token, the host's `auth.json` was left untouched — so every subsequent codex spawn copied a dead token and failed with `refresh_token_reused`. The failure is silent at the user level: `messages_in` get marked `completed`, no outbound row is written, and the operator just sees "the agent went quiet."

Hit in practice this week — a fresh codex agent spawned ~2.5h after the first one of the day stayed silent through three consecutive operator check-ins. Container logs showed the auth manager retrying `refresh_token_reused` on every poll.

## How it works

```diff
- fs.copyFileSync(hostAuth, path.join(codexDir, 'auth.json'));
+ mounts.push({
+   hostPath: hostAuth,
+   containerPath: '/home/node/.codex/auth.json',
+   readonly: false,
+ });
```

The container sees the same inode as the host. When codex refreshes its access token in-place, the new tokens are written back through the bind mount to the host file, and the next codex spawn picks them up.

The existing per-session codex dir mount is preserved so `config.toml` rewrites stay session-local (the container rewrites this on every wake with container-appropriate MCP server paths). The file mount overlays cleanly on top.

If the user hasn't run `codex login` yet (no host `auth.json`), the file mount is skipped and codex falls back to `OPENAI_API_KEY` — same behaviour as before for that case.

## How it was tested

- Triggered a fresh codex spawn after the patch
- Verified `/proc/mounts` inside the container shows both the dir mount and the file mount for `auth.json`
- Confirmed host and container see the same inode (`stat -c '%i' /home/adam/.codex/auth.json` vs `docker exec … stat -c '%i' /home/node/.codex/auth.json`)
- Container produced a normal agent reply with zero `refresh_token_reused` / `token_expired` entries in logs

Caveat I haven't been able to verify in a short test: a real token refresh propagating back to the host file requires waiting for the access token to expire (~1h). If codex ever switches to atomic-rename writes for `auth.json`, the file bind mount would silently regress to leaving the host file stale. Worth keeping an eye on if `refresh_token_reused` re-appears.

## Usage

No user-facing changes. Applies automatically to any agent group using `provider: codex`.

prs.body:
<!-- contributing-guide: v1 -->
## Type of Change

- [ ] **Feature skill** - adds a channel or integration (source code changes + SKILL.md)
- [ ] **Utility skill** - adds a standalone tool (code files in `.claude/skills/<name>/`, no source changes)
- [ ] **Operational/container skill** - adds a workflow or agent skill (SKILL.md only, no source changes)
- [x] **Fix** - bug fix or security fix to source code
- [ ] **Simplification** - reduces or simplifies source code
- [ ] **Documentation** - docs, README, or CONTRIBUTING changes only

## Description

Implements `maybeRotateContinuation` on `OpenCodeProvider` with two
rotation conditions, matching the proactive pattern from `ClaudeProvider`:

**1. Host ceiling-kill signal** — on container startup, checks for a
`.clear-provider-session` file written by the host sweep when the
previous container was ceiling-killed (see companion PR on main). Deletes
the file and returns a rotation reason, causing the poll-loop to discard
the stored continuation and start a fresh session.

**2. Age-based rotation** — rotates sessions older than
`OPENCODE_SESSION_MAX_AGE_MS` (default: 90 min). After Google AI
Studio's context cache TTL expires (1 hour), resuming an old session
costs as much as starting fresh — the full context must be re-uploaded
either way. Rotating proactively avoids replaying long conversation
histories for no cache benefit. Configurable so operators can tune to
their provider's actual TTL.

Also adds `getContinuationAge()` to `session-state.ts`, which reads the
existing `updated_at` column on the `session_state` row — no schema
changes required.

**Depends on:** the `host-sweep.ts` + `poll-loop.ts` changes on main
that write the signal file and clear continuations on empty results.

## For Skills

- [ ] SKILL.md contains instructions, not inline code (code goes in separate files)
- [ ] SKILL.md is under 500 lines
- [ ] I tested this skill on a fresh clone

prs.title: feat(providers): add ACP Client Protocol provider
prs.body:
## Summary

Adds an **ACP Client Protocol** provider that lets NanoClaw act as the
editor/client side of the [Agent Client Protocol](https://agentclientprotocol.com)
(JSON-RPC 2.0 over TCP or stdio). Any external AI coding agent that speaks
ACP can be wired to an agent group — no container image rebuild required.

## Protocol overview

ACP Client Protocol defines a JSON-RPC 2.0 exchange between an **editor**
(NanoClaw) and an **agent** (any ACP-compliant AI). The wire format is one
JSON object per line (`\n`-delimited), over either a TCP socket or stdin/stdout.

### Handshake

editor → agent:  initialize
         ← agent: { protocolVersion, agentCapabilities, meta, authMethods }

editor → agent:  session/new  { cwd, mcpServers }
         ← agent: { sessionId }

### Per-message flow

editor → agent:  session/prompt  { sessionId, prompt: [{ type: "text", text }] }
         ← agent: session/update (notification, 0..N)
                   { method: "session/update",
                     params: { sessionId, update: { sessionUpdate: "agent_message_chunk",
                               content: { role, content: [{ type, text }] } } } }
         ← agent: { content: [], stopReason: "end_turn" }   (RPC response)

NanoClaw collects all `agent_message_chunk` text blocks, joins them, and delivers
the assembled message back through the originating channel.

### File callbacks (optional)

If the agent declares `agentCapabilities.fs.readTextFile / writeTextFile`,
it may call back into NanoClaw mid-prompt:

agent → editor (RPC request):  fs/read_text_file  { path }
                ← editor:  { content: "..." }

agent → editor (RPC request):  fs/write_text_file  { path, content }
                ← editor:  {}

All paths are resolved under `/workspace`; requests outside that boundary
are rejected.

### Session resume

`sessionId` is stored in `outbound.db` after each successful exchange.
On the next message NanoClaw sends the same `sessionId` in `session/prompt`.
If the agent returns a session-not-found error, NanoClaw automatically opens
a new session and retries transparently.

### Connection modes

| Mode       | Config key      | How it works |
|------------|-----------------|--------------|
| Subprocess | `command`       | NanoClaw spawns the agent as a child process; JSON-RPC over stdin/stdout |
| TCP        | `host` + `port` | NanoClaw connects to a running agent server |

## Files

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `container/agent-runner/src/providers/acp-client.ts` | Core provider: transport, dispatcher, session lifecycle |
| `container/agent-runner/src/providers/acp-client.test.ts` | 33 unit tests (bun:test) |
| `src/providers/acp-client.ts` | Host-side config reader — injects env vars into the agent container |
| `.claude/skills/add-acp-client-agent/SKILL.md` | Install + wiring skill |

## Example configuration

**Subprocess mode** (`groups/my-acp-agent/acp-client.json`):
```json
{ "command": ["python3", "/path/to/my-agent.py"] }

TCP mode:
{ "host": "host.docker.internal", "port": 7787 }

container.json (set "provider": "acp-client"):
{
  "provider": "acp-client",
  "groupName": "My ACP Agent",
  "assistantName": "My ACP Agent",
  "agentGroupId": "ag-..."
}
```
## Testing

All 33 container tests pass:
cd container/agent-runner && bun test src/providers/acp-client.test.ts

A minimal echo-mode test server (scripts/test-acp-client-server.py) is
included for manual end-to-end verification — run it untracked alongside
a live NanoClaw instance.

prs.title: feat(providers): surface Claude Code skill catalog to non-Claude providers
prs.body:
## Summary

This PR makes Claude Code skills work for non-Claude providers, in two paired commits:

1. **Source-side** — adds `container/agent-runner/src/providers/skill-catalog.ts`, a shared helper (`composeAvailableSkills` / `listAvailableSkills`) that builds a markdown discovery list of skills available to the current group. Wires it into both non-Claude providers shipped on this branch:
   - **Codex** (`codex.ts`) — appended to `baseInstructions` (string-add at thread start).
   - **OpenCode** (`opencode.ts`) — written to `/tmp/nanoclaw-skills-catalog.md` in `buildOpenCodeConfig` and added to the `instructions` array OpenCode natively reads.
2. **Install-side** — updates `.claude/skills/add-codex/SKILL.md` and `.claude/skills/add-opencode/SKILL.md` so the new file is copied into customer installs alongside the provider files. Without this, any merge of commit 1 alone would break `/add-codex` and `/add-opencode` (provider would import a file that wasn't copied → build break).

Both commits ride one branch off `providers` so they merge atomically; neither is safe alone.

## Why

Claude Code natively exposes skills via its `Skill` tool — agents see (name, description) pairs at runtime and `Read` the full SKILL.md body on demand. Non-Claude providers don't have this discovery mechanism, so per-group prompts referencing skills (e.g. "use the make-website skill") — particularly ones authored under Claude and inherited when a group switches providers — currently dangle. The tool doesn't exist, the body isn't loaded, the agent improvises.

This is observable today: any group whose `CLAUDE.local.md` references a skill stops working that recipe the moment the group switches to Codex or OpenCode, even though the SKILL.md is right there at `/app/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`.

## What the discovery list looks like

```
# Available skills

When the user's request matches a skill below, your first action is to `Read /app/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` and follow the recipe inside before doing the work. The skill's instructions take precedence over your defaults for the task it covers.

- **make-website** — Build and publish a website. Use whenever the user asks to make...
- **wiki** — Maintain the persistent course-content wiki for this group...
```

We deliberately don't inline each SKILL.md body — that would be tens of KB of system prompt for a full catalog, most of which won't apply to any given turn. The lazy-load model mirrors what Claude Code does internally and keeps prompt overhead proportional to skill count, not skill size.

## Test plan

- [x] New `skill-catalog.test.ts` covers: empty/missing dir, frontmatter parsing edge cases (no description, no name field, no frontmatter at all, quoted values), deterministic alphabetical sort.
- [x] Existing codex/opencode tests continue to pass.
- [x] Container suite (`bun test` in `container/agent-runner/`) — 86 pass, 0 fail.
- [x] `pnpm exec tsc -p container/agent-runner/tsconfig.json --noEmit` clean.
- [x] Both install skills updated; running `/add-codex` or `/add-opencode` against the post-merge providers branch will copy the new file. Either skill running second is idempotent (rewrites identical bytes).
- [ ] Manual end-to-end verification on a real Codex agent group (in a downstream fork): the skill catalog appears in the system prompt and the agent invokes the listed skills via `Read`.

## Risk

- **Prompt-size impact:** the discovery list is small (~one line per skill) but it does add to the baseline system prompt for every Codex/OpenCode turn. For a default install with ~10 skills it is well under 1KB.
- **Behavior change:** non-Claude agents that previously ignored skill references will now act on them. If anyone is intentionally relying on those references being ignored, this is a breaking change for them — unlikely but worth flagging.
- **OpenCode tmp-file write:** `/tmp/nanoclaw-skills-catalog.md` is per-container, so no cross-session leakage. Failure to write is logged and falls back gracefully (instructions array just doesn't include it).

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

prs.title: fix(provider): forward ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL into opencode container env
prs.body:
## Problem

When using a non-Anthropic OpenCode provider (e.g. DeepSeek, OpenRouter), the SDK reports **"no providers found"** on every query.

Root cause: `registerProviderContainerConfig('opencode', ...)` in `src/providers/opencode.ts` only forwards three env keys into the container:

```ts
for (const key of ['OPENCODE_PROVIDER', 'OPENCODE_MODEL', 'OPENCODE_SMALL_MODEL'] as const) {
```

But `buildOpenCodeConfig()` inside the container also reads `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` to route requests to the correct endpoint (line ~90). Without it, the base URL is never set and the provider initialisation silently fails.

## Fix

Add `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` to the forwarded key list:

```ts
for (const key of ['OPENCODE_PROVIDER', 'OPENCODE_MODEL', 'OPENCODE_SMALL_MODEL', 'ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL'] as const) {
```

## Tested

Verified on a Hetzner CPX22 / Debian 12 installation with `OPENCODE_PROVIDER=deepseek` and `OPENCODE_MODEL=deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash`. Bot was non-functional before this patch; fully functional after.

The `/add-opencode` skill (on this `providers` branch) should also be updated to document that `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` must be set in the host environment alongside `OPENCODE_PROVIDER`/`MODEL` — but that's a separate docs change.

## Context

I have opened several PRs in a short time while running nullclaw as a Slack and Telegram assistant against OpenAI-compatible gateways (DeepSeek, IFM K2). This issue collects them in one place so they can be reviewed, deferred or closed without triaging each one separately. Two of them overlap open maintainer PRs and need a decision from you (see below); the rest are ready for review.

Each item closes a gap where OpenClaw already has the behaviour; the OpenClaw reference is linked per item (permalinks at `fead50a`). Each PR is independent of the others unless noted and based on current `main`; all are green on linux/macos/windows CI, which runs `zig build test --summary all` with 0 failures and 0 leaks. I also trial-merged each onto `main` + #971 and ran the full suite there, so none of them conflicts with #971 landing first.

## Overlaps with existing PRs

Two of my PRs turned out to overlap with open maintainer PRs. I compared them in detail and propose the following, to avoid duplicate review:

prs.title: fix(streaming): hide text tool calls inside reasoning and CLI streams
prs.body:
Tracked in #1066.

# fix(streaming): hide text tool calls inside reasoning and CLI streams

- Branch: `pr-hide-tool-calls`
- Base: `main` (5f1cade)
- Scope: one concern, a shared stream filter that hides text-form tool calls the dispatcher would execute from every live surface, plus the matching strip on the delivered reply and the stored history
- Breaking change: no

## Summary

Some providers emit tool calls in text form instead of as native tool-call events, for example:

```text
<tool_call>{"name":"shell","arguments":{"command":"..."}}</tool_call>
```

The dispatcher parses and executes those text-form calls. The non-streaming path already suppressed the raw markup before it reached the user (merged #296), and merged #761 wired the CLI text stream through the existing `streaming.TagFilter` via `makeCliStreamSink`. Two live surfaces still leaked. The CLI reasoning stream renders `<think>` blocks through `ThinkPassthroughFilter` (`makeCliStreamSinkPassthrough`), which passed the block through verbatim, so a tool call inside streamed reasoning was echoed to the user. The channel and draft surfaces (the a2a SSE stream, the daemon, `channels/max`, `channels/telegram`) already route through `TagFilter`, which stripped the tool call but ended its `<think>` suppression at an in-block close tag, leaking the reasoning tail and a literal `</think>`. Issue #228 is the security report for this class of leak (a tool call visible in chat).

This change hides dispatcher-executable tool-call markup from every live surface:

- A single `streaming.TagFilter` state machine runs over every streamed chunk. It tracks whether it is inside a `text` or `<think>` region, buffers a tool block, and emits only the surrounding prose. Every sink that streamed raw text now passes through it: the a2a SSE stream, the CLI stream (including the reasoning stream), the daemon, `channel_loop`, `channels/max` and `channels/telegram`.
- `streaming.ThinkPassthroughFilter` becomes a thin wrapper over `TagFilter` in `.render` mode, so reasoning rendering and tool-call hiding share one implementation. On `main` the passthrough filter and the tool-call filter are two separate implementations.
- The dispatcher XML parse (`parseDispatcherXmlToolCalls`) and the batch strip (`stripToolCallMarkup`) move to `providers.helpers`, and the stream filter asks the same predicate (`hidesDispatcherBlock`) whether a candidate block is one the dispatcher would execute. The filter and the dispatcher therefore agree on the dialect: the bracket and function-tag forms, mismatched or any-case close tags, and quoted-colon salvaged names.
- A tool-block body is buffered up to `tool_body_max` (16 KiB); beyond that it spills to a heap buffer (`body_heap`, hard limit `tool_body_hard_max` = 1 MiB) so a large call cannot grow a fixed stack buffer. `TagFilter.deinit` frees the spilled buffer, and `deinit` is wired into every streaming context (`SseStreamCtx`, the CLI `CliStreamCtx`, the daemon, `channel_loop`, `channels/max`, the Telegram `StreamCtx`).
- The close-tag scan is linear (`CloseScanner` / `nextToolCallClose`), so a chunk that ends mid-block does not cause quadratic rescanning.
- Reasoning regions are recognised in every spelling a gateway leaks, not just the plain `<think>`/`</think>`: a shared `providers.helpers.scanThinkTag` classifier matches `<thinking>`, the namespaced forms (`<ifm|think>`, `<mm:think>`) and the pipe form (`<|think|>`). The streaming filter and the batch helpers use the same classifier. An *orphan* namespaced or pipe reasoning closer (no opener, e.g. `</ifm|think>`) with a non-empty visible run on both sides marks a leaked reasoning draft, so the batch scanner drops the draft before it (OpenClaw's `hasOrphanReasoningCloseBoundary` rule) and `stripThinkBlocks`/`splitThinkContent` agree. The plain `</think>` is not a batch drop boundary: a reply may name that tag in prose ("the closing tag is </think>.") and OpenClaw's batch splitter keeps the preceding text there, so the prose is no longer lost. The streaming filter releases the orphan closer verbatim by default, so a snapshot presenter can use it as the drop boundary; an append-only sink (the CLI's stdout, an A2A SSE stream) selects `.suppress` and drops the raw tag instead. A tool block opened inside a namespaced reasoning region now ends at the namespaced closer, and `<think` only opens a region with its `>` delimiter, so prose such as "<think twice before you answer>" stays ordinary text.
- The XML `function` tool dialect is hidden too. `<function>`/`<function_calls>`/`<invoke>`/`<parameter>` blocks and a degenerate run of `</function>`/`</function_calls>` closers are stripped by both the streaming `TagFilter` and the batch stripper (OpenClaw's `TOOL_CALL_TAG_NAMES`), and `containsToolCallMarkup` detects the runaway closer run — with the run-tag names ordered longest-first, so `</function_calls>` is not shadowed by its `</function` prefix — without dropping a reply that merely discusses or quotes the markup.
- The final reply and the stored history no longer carry the markup either. `composeFinalReply` strips tool-call markup from `base_text` before delivery, exactly as it already strips the reasoning quote, and the turn loop stores the same markup-free text it delivers — at the final append and at the forced-follow-through and mid-turn-injection appends — so a re-render of history cannot leak a closer and the model cannot re-read its own garbled text tool call.
- The batch path is Markdown-aware. `findCodeRegionsForToolMarkup` / `isInsideCode` skip fenced blocks and inline spans, so a documented `<function_calls>` sample is preserved verbatim and a fenced three-closer sample no longer blanks the whole reply (which previously aborted the turn with `error.NoResponseContent`). An *unterminated* fence is not code for the tool-markup scan, so a reply that opens ``` and degenerates into a lone `</function>` is still stripped.
- The Max draft preview drops a leaked reasoning draft before an orphan closer, matching Telegram: the streamed buffer is passed through `stripThinkBlocks` before `buildDraftPreviewChunk`.

prs.title: fix(agent): guard structural turn-completion stalls
prs.body:
Tracked in #1066.

## Summary

A model can end a turn with prose that announces the action it is about to take ("Let me check that now") and no tool call. The turn completes with no tool run and no final answer, and the task silently stalls. The existing `shouldForceActionFollowThrough` heuristic (introduced by commit 36e903b, extended in #663 and #908) matches a fixed English/Russian verb list, so it does not generalise to languages without tense or modals — the observed stall is Chinese, where `先把 key 拿出来，改脚本重测。` matches nothing.

This change ports OpenClaw's structural, language-independent guards instead of extending the phrase list:

- **Prompt (`src/agent/prompt.zig`).** `writeToolInstructionsSection` emits an `EXECUTION BIAS` block when tools are present: if the request needs a tool, call it in this turn; saying you are checking, fetching or fixing something is a progress update, not a final answer; never end a turn with only a promise of future work when a tool can act now. It is guarded on `tools.len > 0`, so tool-less prompts are untouched.
- **Providers (`src/providers/{root,anthropic,compatible}.zig`).** `ChatResponse` gains `finish_tool_use`, recorded from provider output structure and never from assistant prose: `finish_reason == "tool_calls"` (OpenAI-compatible) and `stop_reason == "tool_use"` (Anthropic).
- **Agent (`src/agent/root.zig`).** When `finish_tool_use` is set but no call was parsed, the agent nudges once with a tool-use-specific nudge and then fails with `error.NoResponseContent` (already user-visible). Pre-fix this shape had no structural signal, so it fell into the generic empty-response retry — the same nudge-then-fail, but with the generic nudge text; the new test pins which nudge is selected. Two further empty-turn shapes get targeted nudges: settled tools with no user-visible answer (pre-fix the generic retry already recovered these, so the change is the nudge selected, not the recovery), and reasoning-only replies when `reasoning_mode == .off`, which pre-fix failed after a single generic retry (the reasoning is not surfaced as the answer, so it is not a real reply). Each reuses the existing empty-response retry budget, with a cap of 2 for reasoning-only and 1 otherwise.

The `shouldForceActionFollowThrough` list is unchanged. The prose-shaped case ("I'll check now" with `finish_reason: "stop"`) has no structural signal; it is left to the prompt rule.

### Garbled text tool-call markup

A model that falls back to a text tool-call dialect can end a reply with a garbled call the parser cannot turn into an executable one: it announces one more round of work and then emits a lone `</function>` closer, or a bare `<function=name>` opener that never closes. The delivered reply was assembled verbatim, so the markup reached the user (prod: K2 over the OpenAI-compatible gateway, a reply ending in "...电池容量是换算的关键。\n</function>"). The follow-up commits add:

- **Providers (`src/providers/helpers.zig`).** `hasOrphanToolCallClose` — a structural, language-independent signal: an unbalanced tool-call close tag, an unclosed OpenAI `=`-dialect opener (`<function=NAME>` / `<parameter=NAME>`), or a stray `[/tool_call]` bracket closer, outside Markdown code fences and inline spans, with a balanced pair (`<function>...</function>`) treated as prose so a prose mention does not trigger a retry. `stripToolCallMarkup` removes the markup from a reply while preserving code; `hasToolCallMarkup`, `findCodeRegions`/`findCodeRegionsForToolMarkup` and `isInsideCode` back them.
- **Reply assembly (`src/agent/commands.zig`).** `composeFinalReply` routes its base text through `stripToolCallMarkup`, so the delivered reply never carries the markup, exactly as the reasoning quote already is. The streaming preview does not hide this dialect — `src/streaming.zig` TagFilter only suppresses `<tool_call*>`/`<tool_result*>`/`<think*` — so this final-reply strip is the only guard for it; the streaming half is a separate follow-up.
- **Agent (`src/agent/root.zig`).** The turn loop keys a bounded retry (its own counter, cap 1) on `hasOrphanToolCallClose`, reusing the existing nudge machinery with a tool-call-markup-specific nudge; the assistant history entry and the autosave memory summary are stored markup-free, so a re-render cannot leak the closer and the model does not re-read its own garbled call. If the shape recurs, the reply is delivered with the markup stripped, never verbatim.

### Related upstream work

- #663 (merged) "fix(agent): enable empty-response retry and follow-through guardrail in streaming" removed the `!is_streaming` guard from the empty-response retry and the `shouldForceActionFollowThrough` block, and expanded its verb list. #585 (closed) was the superseded duplicate.
- #908 (merged) "Project hktn" expanded the `shouldForceActionFollowThrough` phrase list with more English and Russian search phrasings, extended the empty-response retry nudge to push `web_search`, and added the "External Information and Web Search" section to the system prompt. Both it and #663 stay phrase-list based.
- commit 36e903b (merged in PR #123) "feat(agent): enforce follow-through for deferred action promises" introduced the deferred-action follow-through guardrail this change generalises.
- #584 (merged) "return NoResponseContent when all fields are null/empty" is the `error.NoResponseContent` this change reuses for the tool-use-without-call stop.
- #1050 (open) "add reasoning_mode to surface reasoning-only responses" is the reasoning-only surface this change guards against when reasoning is off.
- Prior-art search (open and closed PRs, issues, all open PR titles) found no PR that keys turn-completion recovery on the provider stop structure (`finish_reason: tool_calls` / `stop_reason: tool_use`) or that injects an execution-bias prompt rule.

### OpenClaw reference

OpenClaw has both halves. The prompt rule is `buildPromisedWorkPromptSection` in `promised-work-prompt.ts` ("Saying \"I am checking/fetching/fixing that now\" is a progress update, not a final answer. Take the next available action in the same turn"). The structural recovery is `incomplete-turn-recovery.ts`: `DEFAULT_REASONING_ONLY_RETRY_LIMIT = 2` and `DEFAULT_EMPTY_RESPONSE_RETRY_LIMIT = 1`, the reasoning-only and settled-tool continuation instructions, and `resolveEmptyResponseRetryInstruction`, which returns `TOOL_USE_WITHOUT_CALL_RETRY_INSTRUCTION` when the assistant stopped with `stopReason === "toolUse"` but no settled tool call ran.

- [promised-work-prompt.ts](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/fead50a35107ed73cbb1f34b93c21716a0583f98/src/agents/promised-work-prompt.ts#L1-L14)
- [incomplete-turn-recovery.ts (limits and instructions)](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/fead50a35107ed73cbb1f34b93c21716a0583f98/src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/incomplete-turn-recovery.ts#L29-L44)
- [incomplete-turn-recovery.ts `resolveEmptyResponseRetryInstruction`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/fead50a35107ed73cbb1f34b93c21716a0583f98/src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/incomplete-turn-recovery.ts#L386-L473)

## Validation

Zig 0.16.0, on this branch (based on current `main` = 5f1cade):

```text
$ zig fmt --check src/
$ zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseSmall
$ zig build test --summary all
Build Summary: 13/13 steps succeeded; 7533/7547 tests passed (14 skipped)
```

### Turn completion (15 tests)

Which fail on pre-fix `main` 5f1cade0 was checked by running each scenario against a pre-fix-equivalent tree. The provider tests and the two agent helper tests (`classifyEmptyResponseNudge`, `emptyResponseNudgeCap`) exercise the new `finish_tool_use` field and helpers, so they cannot compile against pre-fix main. Five of the remaining nine fail pre-fix: the prompt `writeToolInstructionsSection emits EXECUTION BIAS only when tools are present` test (the block is new, so its `EXECUTION BIAS:` assertion fails with `error.TestUnexpectedResult`), the two reasoning-only turn tests (pre-fix the first reasoning-only reply spent the single generic retry: the recovery test fails with `error.NoResponseContent`, and the exhaustion test sees only 2 provider calls instead of 3), and the finish_tool_use and settled-tools turn tests, which fail only on the nudge-text assertion (pre-fix those shapes were retried with the generic empty-response nudge, not the new targeted nudge). The other four pass pre-fix: the tool-less prompt test, and the prose-recovery, settled-tools-exhausted and announcing-prose turn tests (`shouldForceActionFollowThrough`, the generic retry, and a characterization of the untouched shape respectively).

- prompt: `writeToolInstructionsSection emits EXECUTION BIAS only when tools are present`, `buildSystemPrompt omits EXECUTION BIAS when no tools are configured`.
- providers: `parseNativeResponse records finish_tool_use for finish_reason tool_calls` / `... leaves finish_tool_use false for finish_reason stop` (compatible), `parseNativeResponse records finish_tool_use for stop_reason tool_use` / `... leaves finish_tool_use false for stop_reason end_turn` (Anthropic).
- agent: `classifyEmptyResponseNudge prefers reasoning-only then settled-tools then generic`, `emptyResponseNudgeCap allows two reasoning-only retries and one otherwise`, `Agent turn nudges once then fails on finish_tool_use without a tool call`, `Agent turn recovers when finish_tool_use is followed by a real answer`, `Agent turn uses settled-tools nudge and recovers after tools ran`, `Agent turn fails after the settled-tools nudge is exhausted`, `Agent turn retries reasoning-only replies up to two times`, `Agent turn fails after two reasoning-only retries`, and `Agent turn returns announcing prose without a structural retry (step-5 shape)`, which pins the observed Chinese shape: `finish_reason` is `stop`, no structural signal fires, and the prompt rule is the only guard.

### Garbled text tool-call markup (22 tests)

Added by the two markup commits. Their pre-fix behaviour was checked on the parent tree (60ac4b3d): the garbled reply was delivered verbatim after a single provider call.

- providers/helpers: `stripToolCallMarkup drops a single stray function close tag`, `... drops the OpenAI function= dialect block`, `... drops a truncated function= opener`, `... drops an orphan tool_call closer`, `... keeps a function= sample inside a code fence`, `... drops the function_call/function_response and namespaced closers`, `... keeps the prose after an unclosed = opener`, `... drops a lone closer after an unclosed fence`; and `hasOrphanToolCallClose flags the function= dialect shapes`, `... flags a lone namespaced or function_call closer`, `... ignores a balanced pair before a plain unclosed opener`, `... flags a lone closer after an unclosed fence`.
- agent/commands: `composeFinalReply strips a lone orphan tool-call closer from the final answer`, `... strips the orphan closer even with a usage footer`, `... keeps a tool-call sample inside a code fence`.
- agent/root: `Agent turn nudges once on a garbled text tool call and delivers the clean retry`, `... delivers the stripped answer when the text tool call recurs`, `... does not retry a balanced function-markup answer`, `... nudges once on a truncated function= text tool call`, `... delivers the stripped answer when the function= call recurs`, `... stores the history reply free of tool-call markup`, `... nudges on a lone closer after an unclosed fence`.

### Review follow-ups (3 tests)

Three further tests accompany the review fixes; each fails on the tree before its fix, verified by running them on a pre-fix clone (HEAD 77817189) with only the tests added:

- `findCodeRegions returns a sorted, non-overlapping list when a span wraps a fence` — pre-fix the region list was unsorted and overlapping, so `r.start >= prev_end` failed.
- `hasOrphanToolCallClose flags a stray bracket closer` — pre-fix the detector scanned only `<` and returned false.
- `Agent: autosave stores the markup-free reply summary` — pre-fix the stored summary still carried `</function>`.

Pre-fix run: `Build Summary: 11/13 steps succeeded (1 failed); 7530/7547 tests passed (14 skipped, 3 failed)` — exactly the three new tests, nothing else regressed.

Trial-merged onto `main` + #971 (native tool calls while streaming, head 43e0a2d): merges cleanly, no conflicts, and both checks pass:

```text
$ zig fmt --check src/
$ zig build test --summary all
Build Summary: 13/13 steps succeeded; 7548/7562 tests passed (14 skipped)
```

## Notes

- The turn-completion commits change `src/agent/{prompt,root}.zig` and `src/providers/{root,anthropic,compatible}.zig`. No config or API change.
- **Streaming follow-up for #971.** #971 adds native tool calls on the streaming path, where the stop reason arrives as a streamed `finish_reason`. The streaming twin of this change — setting `StreamChatResult.finish_tool_use` from a streamed `finish_reason: "tool_calls"`, detected by scanning the SSE line text (the same approach open PR #1070 uses for a length finish) so a >16 KB data line cannot hide it, and set only when the calls were trusted (clean stream) and the stream was not truncated — is deliberately not included here, because it needs the tool-call-bearing `StreamChatResult.tool_calls` field and the `finalizeStreamResultWithToolCalls` variant, which #971 adds, and the `truncated` flag that #1070 adds. It is prepared as a follow-up for when those land. On plain `main` the non-streaming parsers reach the same `finish_tool_use` branch, so the guard is complete for providers that report a stop reason non-streamed.
- Combines with #971: the two changes both touch `src/agent/root.zig` and `src/providers/{root,anthropic,compatible}.zig`, but trial-merging this branch onto `main` + #971 produces no conflicts and the suite passes (result above).
- The reasoning-only guard fires only when `reasoning_mode == .off`; when reasoning is surfaced as the answer it is a real reply, not a stall.
- The garbled-markup follow-up commits change `src/agent/{commands,root}.zig` and `src/providers/helpers.zig`, and add a `usage.md` FAQ entry (en + zh). No config or API change.
- **Streaming half of the markup guard.** The garbled tool-call markup is stripped only from the final reply; on the live-preview surfaces (CLI, Telegram, MAX) it can still flash while streaming, because `src/streaming.zig` TagFilter only hides `<tool_call*>`/`<tool_result*>`/`<think*`. Teaching TagFilter the `</function>`/`<function>`/`<invoke>`/`<parameter>` and `antml:`/`mm:` dialects is a separate follow-up.

# feat(slack): stream outbound replies while they are generated

**Branch:** `feat/slack-outbound-streaming`
**Commit subject:** `feat(slack): stream outbound replies while they are generated`
**Commits:** 6. Base two: 12 files changed, 2044 insertions(+), 14 deletions(-); then 4 files changed, 264 insertions(+), 3 deletions(-). Follow-ups: `fix(streaming)` 2 files, +52/-3; `fix(daemon)` 2 files, +74/-2; `fix(slack)` drop a stopped turn's queued chunks, 2 files, +130/-0; `fix(slack)` keep native streams under the per-message cap, 4 files, +173/-9.
**Risk tier:** high per `AGENTS.md` section 5 (config schema). The behavior itself is opt-in and default-off. The base two commits add no interface changes; the follow-up adds one optional vtable slot (`Channel.cancelStreams`, default `null`), which every existing channel ignores.

## What changed

Slack was the only streaming-capable channel without an outbound stream sink. `Channel.VTable.sendEvent` with its `.chunk` / `.final` `OutboundStage`, and `supportsStreamingOutbound`, already existed in `src/channels/root.zig`, and Telegram already implemented both, but the Slack vtable registered neither. A Slack reply therefore appeared only once the model had finished, and an operator watching a long turn had no way to tell "still generating" from "stuck".

This change adds a per-account `streaming` key, implements the two vtable hooks on `SlackChannel`, and puts the turn-level state machine in a new transport-free module so it can be tested without HTTP.

### Files changed

| File | Change | +/- |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `src/channels/slack_stream_presenter.zig` | New. Transport-free logic for one streaming turn: transport selection, target parsing, the coalescing window, the late-chunk grace window, the four request bodies, failure classification, and length splitting. 28 tests. | +767 / -0 |
| `src/channels/slack.zig` | `streaming_enabled`, `native_stream_disabled`, `stream_states` and the mutex that guards them; `sendEvent` / `supportsStreamingOutbound`; the native and fallback transports; `streamFinal` reconciliation; `callSlackApi`; `appendPostMessageBody` takes `thread_ts` explicitly. 17 tests. | +733 / -3 |
| `src/config_types.zig` | `streaming: bool = false` on `SlackConfig`, with a doc comment naming the feature gate and the fallback. | +5 / -0 |
| `src/config.zig` | Four tests: the key defaults to false when absent, parses true when present, and appears in the saved config for both values. | +68 / -0 |
| `docs/en/configuration.md` | New `### Slack` section (the page had none) with the parameter list, `#### Slack streaming replies`, `#### Live reasoning in drafts`, the required Slack app settings, verification commands, and common issues. | +107 / -0 |
| `docs/zh/configuration.md` | The same section in Chinese, kept in sync with the English page. | +83 / -0 |
| `src/daemon.zig` | `channelShowsLiveReasoning`; `makeStreamingSinkForChannel` gains a `stream_reasoning` argument and builds the tag filter with the matching think mode; `processInboundMessage` decides it from the outbound channel and the session. 3 tests. | +59 / -5 |
| `src/streaming.zig` | `ThinkMode` (`strip` / `passthrough`), `TagFilter.initWithThinkMode`, and the `inside_think` filter state that forwards a reasoning body verbatim while still stripping tool-call markup. 5 tests. | +103 / -2 |
| `src/providers/helpers.zig` | `quoteThinkBlocks` renders `<think>` blocks as `>`-quoted lines for live drafts; the delivered reply still goes through `stripThinkBlocks`. 4 tests. | +77 / -0 |
| `src/channels/telegram_draft_presenter.zig` | `snapshotDraftText` uses `quoteThinkBlocks` instead of `stripThinkBlocks`. 2 tests. | +30 / -4 |
| `src/session.zig` | `SessionManager.streamsReasoning(session_key)`, a read-only query used to decide whether a draft may render reasoning. | +11 / -0 |
| `src/providers/root.zig` | Re-export `quoteThinkBlocks`. | +1 / -0 |

Two consequences of wiring that sink are worth calling out:

- The draft-side reasoning plumbing: `ThinkMode` in `src/streaming.zig`, `quoteThinkBlocks` in `src/providers/helpers.zig`, the daemon's channel gate, the `streamsReasoning` query, and the Telegram draft presenter. When a session streams reasoning (`/reasoning stream`) and the outbound channel renders it, the thinking is forwarded to the draft and rendered as a quote above the in-progress answer. The delivered reply is unchanged, because the provider still strips think blocks from the final content and `.off` / `.on` previews stay stripped as before. The Notes section below records two gaps in this half.
- A Slack turn that streamed reasoning rewrites the stopped message in place instead of posting the reply a second time, because that turn's draft contains text the final reply omits.

## Why it changed

The outbound staging the daemon needs already existed; only the channel side was missing. Filling it in for Slack is the smallest change that removes the last channel where a reply is delivered in one lump, and it reuses the interface every other streaming channel already goes through instead of adding a Slack-specific path in the agent loop.

Slack's own constraints are why one transport is not enough, and why the implementation carries an account-level degradation flag rather than a single happy path:

- `chat.startStream` is only accepted inside a thread, so a top-level reply can never use the native methods.
- The native methods are gated behind the app's Agents & AI Apps feature, which requires a paid plan, and behind the assistant scope Slack adds when an app is declared as an agent. An app without them cannot stream at all.
- The streaming methods are tiered per minute, so a naive implementation that forwards every model token as one API call would hit the rate limit and break replies that used to work.

## The two outbound paths

`vtableSendEvent` receives `.chunk` events while the model generates and one `.final` event with the authoritative reply. The transport is chosen once per turn and stored on the turn's `StreamState`:

| Reply target | Transport |
| --- | --- |
| Threaded target: `reply_to_mode = all`, an inbound thread reply, or an assistant thread | `chat.startStream` with the first snapshot, throttled `chat.appendStream` deltas, then `chat.stopStream` |
| Top-level target | `chat.postMessage` with the first snapshot, then throttled `chat.update` edits of that same message |
| Any target, once the account has hit a permanent native error | `chat.postMessage` plus `chat.update` |
| Any target, when a native call fails mid-turn | The turn stays on the native transport so the stream can still be closed with `chat.stopStream`; live updates stop and the final reply reconciles the message |

**Native path.** The first flush splits at the `markdown_text` cap and sends it through `chat.startStream`, which returns the streaming message `ts`. Later flushes send only the unsent suffix through `chat.appendStream`, computed from the last snapshot handed to the transport. On `.final`, `pendingFinalSuffix` checks whether the streamed snapshot is a prefix of the final reply. When it is, the remainder is appended and `chat.stopStream` closes the message, so the user sees one message and no duplicate. When it is not, the stream is closed and the reply is delivered separately, because the streamed message holds an intermediate prefix the model later abandoned (text emitted before a tool call, or a reply rewritten by redaction rehydration after the last delta). The one exception is a turn that rendered reasoning: that snapshot can never be a prefix of the final reply, so the stopped message is rewritten in place with `chat.update` instead of leaving the thinking behind and posting the reply a second time.

**Fallback path.** One `chat.postMessage` carries the first snapshot and returns its `ts`; every later flush edits that message with `chat.update`. On `.final`, the reply is split at the `chat.update` cap, the first slice replaces the message, and up to eight overflow slices are posted as follow-ups in the same thread with a warning logged if more are dropped.

`chat.stopStream` is sent with the channel and `ts` only. The content was already delivered through start and append, so passing `markdown_text` there would append it twice.

## Throttling

Slack's streaming Web API methods are tiered per minute, so a token stream must be coalesced before it becomes HTTP calls. The tier table is recorded next to the constants: `chat.startStream` and `chat.stopStream` at Tier 2 (20+ per minute), `chat.appendStream` at Tier 4 (100+ per minute), `chat.update` at Tier 3 (50+ per minute), and `chat.postMessage` at roughly one message per second per channel.

`appendStreamChunk` accumulates deltas in the turn buffer and emits a flush when `STREAM_FLUSH_MIN_INTERVAL_MS` (one second) has elapsed since the previous flush. The one exception is the first flush of a turn: it may open the stream before the interval once the unsent buffer has reached `STREAM_FLUSH_MIN_DELTA_BYTES` (128 bytes), so a burst that arrives before the first tick is not held back for the rest of the second. Every later flush waits the full interval, so a turn costs at most one API call per second per target, which keeps `chat.appendStream` and `chat.update` inside their tiers. (The first version of this patch returned true on the byte threshold before checking the interval, which let the threshold bypass the floor; the `fix(streaming)` follow-up below corrects that.) The window opens on the first delta rather than on the first flush, so a short reply that completes inside one second never opens a stream at all and never pays the Tier 2 start/stop pair. Whitespace-only snapshots are not sent.

Two further guards keep the call count bounded in a long-running bot. A finalized target keeps ignoring `.chunk` events for `STREAM_LATE_CHUNK_GRACE_MS` (five seconds), because the daemon publishes the final reply on the durable outbox worker while the outbound dispatcher may still be draining deltas of the same turn; without it those leftovers would open a second stream for a turn that already ended. Above `STREAM_MAX_TRACKED_TARGETS` (64) tracked targets, the channel sweeps finalized entries that are past the grace window, so a bot does not accumulate one entry per thread it has ever answered in.

`stream_mu` covers both the state map and the API calls made from it, since chunks arrive on the outbound dispatcher thread while the final reply may arrive on the outbox worker.

## Follow-up commits

Four commits tighten the streaming path. Each carries a regression test that was shown to fail before the fix.

| Commit | Files | +/- |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `fix(streaming)`: throttle streamed deltas to the one-second flush floor | `src/channels/slack_stream_presenter.zig`, `src/channels/slack.zig` | +52 / -3 |
| `fix(daemon)`: bound stream-chunk publishing so a stalled channel cannot park the turn | `src/bus.zig`, `src/daemon.zig` | +74 / -2 |
| `fix(slack)`: drop a stopped turn's queued stream chunks | `src/channels/root.zig`, `src/channels/slack.zig` | +130 / -0 |
| `fix(slack)`: keep native streams under the per-message cap | `src/channels/slack.zig`, `src/channels/slack_stream_presenter.zig`, `docs/en/configuration.md`, `docs/zh/configuration.md` | +173 / -9 |

**`fix(streaming)` — the flush floor was bypassable.** The Throttling section above documented a one-flush-per-second floor, but `shouldFlush` returned true on the byte threshold first, so a delta of 128 bytes or more flushed immediately and the interval was never reached. A 360 tok/s stream issued roughly 35 synchronous `chat.appendStream` calls per second, each a fresh TLS connection under `stream_mu` on the single outbound dispatcher thread. Only the first flush of a turn may now use the byte threshold; every later flush waits the full interval. Regression test: a sustained stream of 128-byte deltas flushes once inside the window and again only after it — the pre-fix code flushes on every delta, so the test fails without the change.

**`fix(daemon)` — a full outbound queue parked the turn.** `publishStreamingChunk` published each preview with the blocking `publishOutbound`. Once the bounded outbound queue (`QUEUE_CAPACITY = 100`) filled behind a slow channel call, the agent turn parked in publish and stayed `turn_running`, and the already-queued deltas then replayed before the final. Stream chunks are now published through a new `Bus.publishOutboundTimeout` with a zero timeout, so a preview is dropped the moment the queue is full instead of blocking the turn; the final reply still uses the reliable blocking publish. Regression tests: `publishOutboundTimeout` reports `Timeout` on a full queue instead of blocking, and `publishStreamingChunk` drops the preview and returns — with the pre-fix blocking publish the second test parks on the full queue and hangs.

**`fix(slack)` — a stopped turn's queued chunks could replay.** After a `/stop`, deltas already queued ahead of the stop must not reach the user once the dispatcher catches up. `SlackChannel` now keeps a per-target cancel marker (`stream_cancels`, guarded by `stream_mu`, expiring after `STREAM_LATE_CHUNK_GRACE_MS`) and drops a cancelled target's `.chunk` events before the transport. The marker is cleared when the stopped turn's final reply is delivered — including a turn that streamed nothing — and on stop, so it cannot leak into the next turn. Regression tests: a cancelled target drops a delta that would otherwise flush past the interval, and a positive control proves the same clock advance without a cancel lets the delta through.

**`fix(slack)` — the native stream ignored Slack's cumulative message cap.** Slack caps the whole streamed message, not just each `chat.appendStream` call, so a turn that kept every call under the per-call 12,000-char cap (`STREAM_MARKDOWN_MAX_BYTES`) could still make a later append answer `msg_too_long`; a per-call split cannot prevent a cumulative overflow. The flush now reports when the accumulated snapshot has passed a conservative cumulative budget (`STREAM_TOTAL_MAX_BYTES`, the per-call cap reused as a proxy, because Slack documents the per-call cap but not the cumulative one). Past it the native stream is closed and the turn finishes on the edited-message transport (`chat.update` plus thread follow-ups), so the final answer is delivered intact. The closing append in `streamFinal` respects the same budget, and an actual `msg_too_long` from `chat.appendStream` also closes the stream and switches the turn to the fallback transport instead of only dropping live updates — otherwise a turn with no final body could leave its message stuck in the streaming state. Regression tests: a chunk past the budget leaves the native transport, a turn that only crosses the budget on a later flush switches too, and `appendStreamChunk` flags the cumulative overflow — all shown to fail on the pre-fix code.

Interaction with the `/stop` work: the marker is exposed as the optional `Channel.cancelStreams` vtable slot, but the daemon call site that resolves the interrupted session's delivery target and invokes it belongs to the interrupt plumbing tracked in #1068, not to this PR. This PR ships and tests the channel-local half; once #1068 lands, its stop fast-path calls `channel.cancelStreams(target)` with no further change here.

## Permanent errors degrade the account

`classifyStreamFailure` maps the Slack `error` string to a retry policy:

- **Permanent** (`disable_native`): `channel_type_not_supported`, `method_not_supported_for_channel_type`, `unknown_method`, `not_allowed`, `invalid_thread_ts`, `restricted_action_thread_only_channel`, `restricted_action_non_threadable_channel`, `restricted_action_thread_locked`, `missing_scope`, `not_allowed_token_type`, `no_permission`, `restricted_action`, `invalid_arguments`, `missing_recipient_user_id`, `missing_recipient_team_id`. These mean this app, workspace, or channel can never stream natively, so the account sets `native_stream_disabled` once and every later turn selects the fallback transport directly through `chooseTurnTransport`. The warning is logged once per account, not once per turn.
- **Transient** (everything else, including `ratelimited`, `internal_error`, `service_unavailable`, and `message_not_in_streaming_state`): the current turn abandons the native path and the API is retried on a later turn. Unknown codes are treated as transient, so a Slack error that did not exist when this was written can never permanently disable streaming for an account.

A rejection of the start call switches the current turn to the fallback transport. A failure of a later append or update sets `send_failed` for that turn, which stops live updates and leaves the final reply to reconcile the message. If the first `chat.postMessage` of a fallback turn fails, the same flag applies and the reply is sent complete through the existing `vtableSend` path. In every failure case the user still receives the reply; the only difference is whether it arrives progressively.

## Configuration

New key, `channels.slack.accounts.<alias>.streaming`, default `false`:

```json
{
  "channels": {
    "slack": {
      "accounts": {
        "<alias>": {
          "bot_token": "YOUR_BOT_TOKEN",
          "app_token": "YOUR_APP_TOKEN",
          "reply_to_mode": "all",
          "streaming": true
        }
      }
    }
  }
}
```

The key is documented in `docs/en/configuration.md` and in `docs/zh/configuration.md`. Both pages state the app-side requirements for the native path: enable **Agents & AI Apps** under *Features* (the gate for `chat.startStream`, and a paid-plan feature), keep `chat:write` for outbound replies and `assistant:write` for the assistant scope, reinstall the app after changing scopes, and set `reply_to_mode` to `all` if replies in channels should stream, since Slack only streams inside a thread.

## Backward compatibility

- The key defaults to `false`. A configuration that does not mention it parses to `false`, and the saved configuration writes the effective value.
- With streaming off, `supportsStreamingOutbound` returns `false`, so the daemon never routes Slack through the outbound staging, and `sendEvent` forwards `.final` to the existing `vtableSend` while ignoring `.chunk`. Delivery is byte-for-byte what it is today.
- `appendPostMessageBody` now takes `thread_ts` as an argument instead of reading the mutable `self.thread_ts` field that `parseTarget` rewrites. The existing call site passes the same value the function read before, so the payload is unchanged.
- `Channel.cancelStreams` is an optional vtable slot defaulting to `null`, so a channel that does not implement it is unaffected; only Slack registers it, and only the daemon's `/stop` fast-path (from #1068) calls it.
- No state is persisted. Stream state lives in the channel instance, is released per turn by `finishTurn`, and is freed on `stop`.
- No new command, flag, or migration, and no change to the config file layout.

## Rollback

Set `streaming` to `false` (or remove the key) and restart the channel; replies go back to being delivered complete. `git revert <this-commit-sha>` also works, and no data migration or cleanup is needed because nothing is persisted.

## Security

- No new credentials. The streaming methods authenticate with the bot token the account already has, through the existing `Authorization: Bearer` header built in a fixed stack buffer.
- No new scope is required for the fallback path: `chat.postMessage` and `chat.update` are covered by `chat:write`, which outbound replies already need. The native methods are the same scope but are additionally gated on the app's Agents & AI Apps feature and the assistant scope, as both doc pages state. Enabling `streaming` without that entitlement cannot break replies, because the first `chat.startStream` is rejected and the account degrades to edited messages.
- No new endpoints. Requests go through the existing `root.http_util.curlPost` to the existing Slack Web API base over HTTPS.
- No new inbound surface. The change adds no webhook, listener, or event parser.
- No new file, filesystem, or subprocess access.
- No secrets in logs. Failure paths log the Slack error code, the endpoint name, and the Zig error name only; message bodies and tokens are not logged. The token never leaves the auth header.
- Under `builtin.is_test`, `sendMessage` returns before building a request and `callSlackApi` returns a canned `ts`, so the suite opens no sockets. Both guards carry a comment, per the `builtin.is_test` side-effect rule in `AGENTS.md` section 3.4.
- Tests and docs use synthetic values (`xoxb-test`, `xoxb-YOUR_BOT_TOKEN`, and example channel and user ids), not real credentials or workspace identifiers.

## Validation

Required checks for a code change, both run in CI on the pinned Zig 0.16.0 toolchain:

- `zig build test --summary all` (the `pre-push` hook in `.githooks`; must report 0 failures and 0 leaks)
- `zig fmt --check src/` (the `pre-commit` hook in `.githooks`)

Both commands are green on the pinned Zig 0.16.0 toolchain:

- CI (PR head `2dc6ca4b`): [run 38964844012](https://github.com/nullclaw/nullclaw/actions/runs/38964844012) — 3/3 jobs passed (`linux-x86_64`, `macos-aarch64`, `windows-x86_64`), each running `zig build test --summary all`.
- Local (Zig 0.16.0 container), with the four follow-up commits: `zig fmt --check src/` clean; `zig build test --summary all` reports `Build Summary: 13/13 steps succeeded; 7574/7588 tests passed (14 skipped)`, 0 failures and no leaks.

Each follow-up commit's regression test was confirmed to fail before its fix: reverting `shouldFlush` fails `appendStreamChunk throttles a sustained delta stream to one flush per interval` (and the updated `slack streaming keeps the native path across chunks of one turn`); neutralizing the cancel check fails `slack streaming drops queued chunks for a cancelled target` while its positive control still passes; reverting `publishStreamingChunk` to the blocking publish parks the `publishStreamingChunk drops a preview ...` test on the full queue; and reverting the cumulative-budget check (the `native_full` flag and the `streamFinal` budget guard) fails `slack native stream finishes on the fallback transport past the message budget`, `slack native stream leaves for the fallback transport when a later flush crosses the budget`, and `appendStreamChunk flags the native stream full once the turn crosses the budget` — on the pre-fix tree the suite reports `7571/7588 tests passed (14 skipped, 3 failed)`, exactly those three.

Test coverage added by this change (73 test blocks):

| File | Tests | What they exercise |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `src/channels/slack_stream_presenter.zig` | 32 | Transport selection across the four target/state combinations; target parsing for a threaded, bare, empty-thread, and DM-style target; the coalescing window (buffered inside it, interval flush, byte-threshold flush, unsent-suffix delta) and the sustained-stream throttle that keeps the interval floor; the late-chunk grace window and the fresh turn after it; prefix versus divergent finals; all four request bodies including JSON escaping and the stop body carrying no text; permanent versus transient classification; length splitting at newline boundaries and without cutting a multibyte character; and the cumulative-budget guard (a short snapshot is not flagged full, two flushes that each stay under the per-call cap trip the flag once their sum passes the message budget, and `finalAppendOverflowsBudget` guards the closing append) |
| `src/channels/slack.zig` | 21 | The vtable hooks and the full state machine, driven with `callSlackApi` stubbed: native start for a thread target, native kept across chunks, fallback for a top-level target, fallback after the account is degraded, prefix final, divergent final, in-place rewrite after streamed reasoning, late deltas dropped, streaming disabled, empty chunk, short reply inside the window, overflow splitting, `stop` releasing buffers, a cancelled target dropping a queued chunk plus its positive control, and a chunk past the message budget (or a later flush that crosses it) leaving the native transport for the fallback one |
| `src/bus.zig` | 1 | `publishOutboundTimeout` reports `Timeout` on a full queue instead of blocking, and accepts again once an entry is drained |
| `src/daemon.zig` | 4 | The sink keeps reasoning only when the session streams it, strips it by default, the channel gate enables only Telegram and Slack, and `publishStreamingChunk` drops a preview when the outbound queue is full |
| `src/streaming.zig` | 5 | Strips think blocks by default, forwards them in passthrough mode, survives a tag split across chunks, keeps angle brackets inside reasoning, and still strips tool-call markup in passthrough mode |
| `src/providers/helpers.zig` | 4 | Quote rendering that keeps the answer, plain text untouched, an unterminated block, and a stray close tag |
| `src/config.zig` | 4 | The key defaults to false when absent, parses true when present, and appears in the saved configuration for both values |
| `src/channels/telegram_draft_presenter.zig` | 2 | Streamed reasoning renders as a quote, and a draft without reasoning is unchanged |

The new Slack section in both doc pages also carries manual verification steps (`nullclaw channel start slack`, `nullclaw channel status`). Those require a live Slack app and were not run in the environment where this description was written.

## Notes

- Six commits. The first adds the Slack outbound stream and the shared draft-side plumbing for streamed reasoning, which belong together because both are served by the one outbound sink this PR adds: the same `.chunk` events feed the Slack stream and the draft renderers. The second fixes that plumbing on the channels with their own message loop and is a hard dependency of the first. The four follow-ups tighten the streaming path — the flush floor, the bounded chunk publish, dropping a stopped turn's queued chunks, and keeping the native stream under Slack's per-message cap — and are the parts of the `/stop` / backpressure work tracked in #1068 that belong to the Slack outbound stream. Happy to narrow the scope however maintainers prefer.
- The second commit fixes the channels that are served by their own message loop. Telegram is served by `channel_loop.processTelegramMessage` rather than `daemon.processInboundMessage`, so the passthrough selection the daemon performs never ran for it and its drafts were always stripped; the draft think mode is now resolved from the outbound channel and the session, the same way the daemon already does it. That commit also teaches `TagFilter` the provider's text tool markup, which otherwise reaches drafts and delivered replies verbatim. It is in this branch rather than a PR of its own because it cannot compile without the first commit: the `ThinkMode` and `initWithThinkMode` symbols it consumes, and the daemon-side channel gate, are introduced here.
- The `fix(slack)` follow-up adds the `Channel.cancelStreams` vtable slot and the Slack-local cancel marker, but deliberately not the daemon call site that drives them: that resolution (which outbound target a `/stop` should cancel) is part of the interrupt plumbing in #1068. Until #1068 lands the slot has no caller in the daemon, so the channel-local behaviour is covered by its unit tests rather than an end-to-end `/stop` test.
- Reasoning in a draft is presentation-only. The finalized message is still produced by `stripThinkBlocks`, so thinking never reaches a delivered reply in any mode.
- The native path needs the app's Agents & AI Apps feature, which requires a paid plan. On a workspace without it, `streaming = true` is harmless: the first start call is rejected, the warning is logged once per account, and replies use edited messages.
- Behavior worth knowing when reviewing the native path: a final reply that diverges from the streamed text is posted as its own message, so that turn produces two messages. This is deliberate, because the streamed message holds an intermediate prefix that the model abandoned, and the reply has to be complete. The one exception is a turn that rendered reasoning, which is rewritten in place.
- On scope: the `fix(channels)` commit is not a separate concern bolted on. The streamed Slack output both depends on and exposes that plumbing — it selects the draft think mode per channel and strips the provider's text tool markup — so it stays in this PR to keep the change self-contained and compilable. If the maintainer prefers a narrower diff, I am happy to split it into its own PR after this one lands.

prs.title: feat(slack): handle a single Slack slash command over Socket Mode
prs.body:
Tracked in #1066.

## Problem

In Socket Mode, Slack sends a slash command as a `slash_commands` envelope. `handleSocketPayload` acks every envelope but only processes `events_api` envelopes, so slash-command envelopes are dropped silently. A registered command, for example `/nullclaw /stop`, therefore does nothing. Slack shows no error either, because the envelope was acked.

## Change

- New opt-in setting per account: `channels.slack.accounts.<id>.slash_command` `{ enabled, name }`. It is disabled by default. The default name is `nullclaw`; the name is compared without the leading `/` and ignoring case.
- The handler acks the envelope first, to stay within Slack's 3 s budget. It then checks that the command name matches and applies the same DM and group allowlist checks as an ordinary message. If both pass, `payload.text` is published to the bus as a top-level message in `payload.channel_id`. Any text therefore works, including control commands such as `/stop`, `/new` and `/think`, which the existing slash-command layer handles as if they had been typed.
- Replies the user would otherwise never see are sent as ephemeral messages via `response_url`, with the POST capped at 2 s so it cannot stall the socket loop:
  - usage text when the command has no text
  - a refusal when the sender is not allowed
  - a notice when the command name does not match the configured one (also logged)
- Envelopes with `retry_attempt > 0` are ignored, so a failed ack cannot run the same command twice.
- A slash command is an explicit invocation of the app, so it counts as a mention for `group_policy = mention_only`. Allowlists are still enforced. The docs say this explicitly, so operators can tighten `allow_from` if needed.
- The end of `processHistoryMessage` that publishes the inbound message is moved into `publishInboundMessage`, so both paths derive `chat_id` and `session_key` the same way.

OpenClaw has the same single-command model: `channels.slack.slashCommand` `{ enabled, name, sessionPrefix, ephemeral }`. The handler is registered in [slash.ts](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/fead50a35107ed73cbb1f34b93c21716a0583f98/extensions/slack/src/monitor/slash.ts) and the config is resolved in [commands.ts](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/fead50a35107ed73cbb1f34b93c21716a0583f98/extensions/slack/src/monitor/commands.ts). The behaviour is documented in [messaging.md](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/fead50a35107ed73cbb1f34b93c21716a0583f98/docs/channels/slack/messaging.md).

## Notes

- **Interrupting a running turn.** On current `main`, a `/stop` sent while a turn is already running is still dropped by the inbound router. That applies to typed messages too, and #1068 fixes it on every channel. This PR only makes sure the command reaches the bus.
- **Retry handling.** Ignoring retries assumes the first delivery was processed. If the socket drops before an envelope is read, the redelivered copy is ignored. Deduplicating by `envelope_id` instead would cover that case; I can switch to it if you prefer.

## Setup

App manifest:

```json
"features": {
  "slash_commands": [
    { "command": "/nullclaw", "description": "Send a message to nullclaw", "should_escape": false }
  ]
}
```

The bot also needs the `commands` scope. In Socket Mode the request URL is not used.

## Tests

`zig fmt --check src/` is clean, and `zig build test --summary all` passes (13/13 steps, 0 failures, 0 leaks). New tests cover:
- name matching
- the published message
- `/stop` reaching the agent stop handler
- an unknown command name
- the refusal for a sender who is not allowed
- empty text
- ack before dispatch
- retry suppression
- the response body encoding
- config parsing and defaults

prs.title: fix(channels): bound channel network I/O and make poller supervision non-blocking
prs.body:
Tracked in #1066.

## Summary

Every network call that can run on a channel polling thread is now time-bounded,
and a wedged poller can no longer hang its own supervision.

**Incident.** After a Telegram turn the poller stopped advancing `last_activity`;
the supervisor reported `polling thread stale` 33 minutes later, and the restart
that followed deadlocked in `std.Thread.join()` until a manual container restart.

**Root cause.** `telegram_api.Client.post` discarded its timeout argument
(`_ = timeout;`) and forwarded to `http_util.httpPostJsonWithProxy`, which uses
`std.http.Client`. Zig 0.16's `std.http` has no client-side socket read timeout,
so a connection silently dropped mid-flight (no FIN/RST) blocks the read until
the kernel's TCP keepalive fires (default 2h). `getUpdates` (30s long poll),
`setMessageReaction` and the typing/draft calls all run on the poller thread and
all shared that path. The same class of bug was reachable on the other polling
channels — voice transcription's `getFile` runs inside `pollUpdates`, and
signal/matrix/weixin/max run unbounded calls inside their poll loops and
reply-send paths. A second, independent failure was in supervision itself:
`ChannelManager.stopPollingThread` called `t.join()` with no timeout, so a wedged
poller deadlocked the supervision loop instead of being restarted.

### Bounded channel I/O

Route every call that can run on a polling thread through a curl `--max-time`
transport so a stalled socket returns `error.CurlTimeout` within the bound
instead of hanging.

- `http_util`: add `httpRequestWithTimeout`, `httpRequestWithStatusTimeout`,
  `httpGetWithProxyTimeout` and `httpPostJsonWithProxyTimeout`. They call
  `secureCurlRequestWithStatusAndHeaders` directly, so they neither fall back to
  the untimed `std.http` client for a credentialed request nor set curl `--fail`
  (a non-2xx keeps `httpRequest`'s `error.HttpStatusError` identity). The bounded
  GET takes an explicit size cap so a media download is not silently truncated at
  the 4 MiB GET default; `DEFAULT_CURL_GET_MAX_BYTES` becomes `pub` for the same
  reason.
- `telegram_api`: `post()` honours its timeout and logs the failing method and
  its bound (a benign `getUpdates` timeout stays at debug); `downloadFile` honours
  its timeout with a 64 MiB cap; `postMultipart` is bounded at 120s; `Client`
  gains an `api_base` override for self-hosted Bot API servers and so the poller
  path can be tested against a local stalled socket.
- `max_api`: `getMe`, `sendMessage`, `editMessage`, `deleteMessage`,
  `answerCallback`, `getUpdates`, `subscribe`/`unsubscribe`, `sendTypingAction`
  and the media upload all run on the Max poller thread (`runMaxLoop` dispatches
  inline); route them through the bounded path. `Client` gains `api_base` /
  `stub` / `write_timeout` overrides for tests.
- `matrix`: `/sync` long poll, `healthCheck` probe, `acceptInvite` auto-join,
  typing and message send are bounded.
- `signal`: attachment fetch plus RPC/REST send and typing are bounded.
- `weixin`: `getupdates` long poll and `sendMessage` are bounded; raise the
  `getupdates` bound to 45s for headroom over the server long poll.
- `voice`: the Telegram `getFile` call inside `pollUpdates` is bounded.

### Non-blocking supervision

- Every polling loop records `exited` as its last action and a coarse `step`
  (`startup`/`polling`/`dispatching`). The supervisor waits for `exited` with a
  bound (`POLLING_STOP_GRACE_NS`, 150s — longer than the largest bound on the
  poller path, a 120s media upload) and detaches a thread that never returns
  (`t.detach()` reclaims its 16 MiB stack) instead of blocking forever; the entry
  is then respawned.
- Replace the previous blanket "don't touch a dispatching poller" with a
  per-step liveness signal so a stall that happens *while dispatching* is still
  recovered. Each loop state gains a poller-owned `progress` heartbeat, refreshed
  when the poll loop enters a dispatch, on every turn progress hint (tool call)
  through a `ProgressSink`, and on streaming channels on every streamed chunk. A
  poller is left alone only while it is dispatching *and* still progressing; a
  dispatching poller whose heartbeat has frozen past `DISPATCH_STALL_SECS`
  (900s) is stopped and detached.
- Telegram keeps worker-turn progress in a separate `turn_progress` cell, so a
  wedged poller whose off-thread worker keeps streaming is still declared stale
  (folding worker progress into poller liveness was the one stall supervision
  could not recover).
- Add a hard wall-clock bound (`MAX_DISPATCH_SECS`, 1800s): a turn that keeps
  emitting progress hints but never finishes is still recovered, since
  `last_activity` only advances on the poll step.
- Diagnostics: the stale log names the poller's step and idle time; a Bot API
  failure names the method and its bound; a respawn logs
  `polling thread started`. A restart deferred because the poller is busy no
  longer counts against the circuit breaker.
- A detached poller that resumes no longer rewinds the persisted Telegram update
  offset, and the poller tears down `tg_ptr.transcriber` only while it still owns
  it, so a detached poller exiting after a respawn does not free the live
  transcriber (voice transcription silently disabled).

### Prior art (OpenClaw)

OpenClaw already bounds its Telegram poller this way, which this change brings
nullclaw toward parity with:

- `extensions/telegram/src/request-timeouts.ts` — a per-method Bot API timeout
  (`getupdates` 45s, `TELEGRAM_LONG_POLL_ABORT_MARGIN_SECONDS` 5s of headroom).
- `extensions/telegram/src/api-fetch.ts` — every request carries a
  `buildTimeoutAbortSignal` / `AbortController` bound and a 4 MiB response cap.
- `extensions/telegram/src/polling-liveness.ts` — a liveness tracker with
  `detectStall({ thresholdMs })` and diagnostic fields (in-flight, outcome,
  started/finished, duration, offset), the analogue of the `step`/`progress`/
  idle diagnostics here.
- `extensions/telegram/src/polling-session.ts` — `POLL_STOP_GRACE_MS` (15s), then
  `stop timed out ...; forcing restart cycle`, and
  `polling-session-restart-policy.ts` backs off a stop-timeout burst. This is the
  same "bounded stop, then restart" shape as `POLLING_STOP_GRACE_NS` + detach +
  respawn.

## Validation

Local WSL docker (`nc-zig:0.16.0`), branch `fix/bounded-channel-io` from
`5f1cade05c`:

```
$ zig fmt --check src/ && zig build test --summary all
Build Summary: 13/13 steps succeeded; 7513/7527 tests passed (14 skipped)
```

Regression tests (each proven to fail against the pre-port behaviour by
reverting the fix in place and re-running the suite):

- Revert `telegram_api.Client.post` to the untimed `httpPostJsonWithProxy` →
  `telegram getUpdates returns a bounded error on a stalled socket` fails with
  `expected error.CurlTimeout, found error.ReadFailed`.
- Revert `http_util.httpGetWithProxyTimeout` to `curlGetWithProxy` (curl `--fail`
  + 4 MiB cap) → `bounded http get maps a non-2xx to HttpStatusError` fails with
  `expected error.HttpStatusError, found error.CurlFailed`, and
  `bounded http get enforces the response size cap` fails.
- Revert `channel_manager.stopPollingThreadGrace` to the blanket dispatch
  suppression → `stopPollingThreadGrace stops a dispatching poller whose
  heartbeat is stale` and `... stops a progressing turn past the hard dispatch
  bound` fail.

The ported tests all carry `// Regression:` comments naming the pre-fix failure.

## Related PRs

- **#134** (merged) added curl timeouts to every Telegram network call. The Bot API client later moved to `std.http`, and `Client.post` / `downloadFile` now discard their `timeout` argument (`_ = timeout;`), so that bound was lost. This PR restores it on the current transport.
- **#984** (open) fixes the opposite blind spot in the same supervisor: a poller whose polls *fail* kept refreshing `last_activity` and was never declared stale. This PR covers a poll that never *returns*, and makes the supervisor's stop bounded so a wedged thread cannot also wedge the supervisor. The two are complementary. A trial merge conflicts textually in `src/channel_manager.zig` only; I will rebase onto whichever lands first.

## Notes

- **One concern.** This is the "bounded channel I/O" concern only. The related
  `max_api`/`weixin`/`matrix`/`signal` bounding is the same bug class on the same
  polling threads and shares the new `http_util` helpers, so it is folded in
  here; the supervision change is what makes a stall recoverable once the
  network calls are bounded. Happy to split if preferred.
- **Residual risks, documented in-code.** After a detach the old and respawned
  poller can briefly overlap (the detached one re-checks `stop_requested` at the
  top of its loop, so it exits as soon as the blocked call returns); worker joins
  stay unbounded on purpose (a timed-out join would detach a hung turn still
  holding its session lock, masking the stall — the heartbeat + supervisor detach
  recovers it instead).
- **Follow-up.** The weixin `getupdates` bound (45s) is a guess: the request
  sends no explicit long-poll timeout and the server default is not documented
  in-tree. A follow-up should send an explicit long-poll timeout in the payload
  (as Telegram and Max do) once the default is known.
- No user-visible config or CLI surface changes, so no docs changes.
