prs.title: fix(agent): honor /stop on every channel and abort the in-flight provider stream
prs.body:
Tracked in #1066.

## Summary

`/stop` only reached a running turn on Telegram. On the daemon/gateway path an inbound `/stop` was treated like any other message, so a stop for a busy session was enqueued behind the running turn on that session's FIFO worker and its `routeInbound` was not reached until the turn it was meant to stop had already finished; when the queue policy was `off` the message was dropped outright (`session busy queue_mode=off`). Even when a stop did land, the provider's curl stream kept running: the turn was flagged interrupted but the in-flight HTTP request streamed to completion.

This change makes `/stop` interrupt a busy session on every channel and abort the in-flight provider stream:

- `SessionManager.routeInbound` consults the control plane's stop predicate before the inbound-routing switch. When the session already has a turn in flight, a stop-like command requests the turn interrupt and the message is dropped (`.skip`) instead of being injected into or queued behind the running turn. This is the central path every channel shares (daemon/Slack, the channel_loop variants, callback queries, the synchronous Telegram path).
- The daemon inbound dispatcher runs the same check on each ready message before it hands the message to a worker, so a stop never waits behind the FIFO queue that holds the work it is cancelling. Routing (shard index and session key) is resolved through shared helpers (`resolveInboundDispatchSessionKey`, `inboundDispatchShardIndex`) so the dispatcher and the worker agree on which session a message belongs to; FIFO is preserved for every non-stop message.
- The provider curl stream installs the same cancel watcher `http_util` already uses for cancellable requests. When the turn is interrupted the watcher kills the child process, which closes the stdout pipe and unblocks the read loop; `curlStream` returns `error.Interrupted`. A `stdin` write failure caused by that kill is recognised as a stop (`stdinWriteFailureIsInterrupt`) rather than reported as a provider write error, and a stream that ends without `[DONE]` while the cancel flag is set returns `error.Interrupted` instead of salvaging the partial text.
- The compatible provider propagates `error.Interrupted` instead of treating it as a stream failure and falling back to a fresh non-streaming request (which silently ignored the stop).
- The agent exposes its interrupt flag to the stream, treats `error.Interrupted` on the streaming path (including the post-vision-error retry) as a user stop and returns the interrupt reply, and re-checks the interrupt flag after a streamed response completes so a stop that arrives mid-stream still ends the turn.

Four follow-up commits extend the abort to every provider route and every stream read loop, so a stop is not limited to the streaming OpenAI-compatible route and does not wait for the read loop to drain:

- **`fix(agent): abort the in-flight provider request on /stop for every route`** — the interrupt flag was only installed inside the `if (is_streaming)` branch, so a turn without a stream sink (the blocking `provider.chat` path, e.g. Telegram with draft streaming off) ran the whole request with a null thread-local and the cancel watcher was never spawned. The flag is now installed for the whole provider call, covering the blocking path, the `reasoning_content` / vision retries and the compaction retries. `error.CurlInterrupted` (raised by the blocking curl transport when the watcher kills the child) is treated as a user stop exactly like `error.Interrupted`, on the streaming branch, the blocking branch and every retry catch. `ReliableProvider` no longer retries or fails over a user stop: `tryChatProvider` returned `?ChatResponse`, so a `CurlInterrupted` from the inner provider was swallowed and the next model/provider was tried; it now propagates `error.Interrupted`.
- **`fix(providers): check the interrupt flag inside every curl stream read loop`** — `curlStream` checked the flag only after the read loop returned, and `curlStreamAnthropic` / `curlStreamGemini` / the OpenAI-Codex stream never checked it and spawned no cancel watcher, so a fast or degenerate stream kept reading (and publishing) deltas for seconds after the stop. All four transports now spawn the same cancel watcher (factored into `http_util.spawnCancelWatcher`, `http_util.stopCancelWatcherAndReap` and `http_util.interruptRequested`) and check the flag at the top of the read loop and between deltas, returning `error.Interrupted` instead of draining what curl already buffered.
- **`fix(daemon): never park a turn publishing a stream chunk to a full outbound queue`** — `publishStreamingChunk` used the blocking `publishOutbound`, so a full outbound queue (a stalled channel call) parked the agent turn behind the dispatcher, keeping it `turn_running` and deaf to `/stop` until the backlog drained. Stream chunks are now published through the new `Bus.publishOutboundTimeout` with a timeout of 0 and dropped the moment the queue is full; the final reply still uses the reliable blocking publish.
- **`fix(telegram): route before the draft turn so /stop does not clobber the live draft`** — `processTelegramMessage` started the typing/draft turn before consulting the inbound router, so a `/stop` folded into the running turn still rotated the chat's draft id, cleared the buffer and then deleted the slot on return, dropping the running turn's later streamed reasoning. Routing now happens first, so a message the router folds into the running turn leaves that turn's live draft (and typing indicator) untouched.

The Slack-specific parts of the same stack (throttling streamed deltas to the presenter's minimum flush interval, and dropping a stopped turn's already-queued chunks) are left to #1058, which owns Slack outbound streaming.

### Related upstream work

- #321 (merged) added the Telegram `/stop` hard-stop: it wires `/stop` and `/abort` to a session interrupt and adds cancellable subprocess/curl execution. That path is Telegram-only and cancels the tool subprocess, not the provider request; this change makes the check channel-independent and aborts the provider stream itself.
- #855 (merged) added session-level preemption: a new message for a busy session requests interrupt before waiting on the lock. That is reached only once the message has been dequeued; here the stop is recognised before enqueue.
- #910 (merged) made the Discord/websocket stop interrupt-safe. #1033 (open) reports cron agent jobs with no default timeout that can block the scheduler indefinitely — the same class of "a long turn with no way to stop it".
- Prior-art search (open and closed PRs, issues, all open PR titles) found no PR that checks `/stop` before the channel queue or that aborts the in-flight provider stream.

### OpenClaw reference

OpenClaw recognises a stop at ingress, before the run machinery. `isAbortRequestText` normalizes the body and matches `/stop` in `abort-primitives.ts`; the shared reply dispatcher resolves it through `tryFastAbortFromMessage`/`resolveFastAbortRequest` in `abort.ts` and only then loads the active-run cancellation path. `shouldPersistAbortCutoff` in `abort-cutoff.ts` handles a targeted `/stop` arriving from a slash/session-control key, and the session record keeps an `abortCutoffMessageSid`/`abortCutoffTimestamp` boundary so the pre-stop queue backlog is skipped rather than replayed.

- [abort-primitives.ts](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/fead50a35107ed73cbb1f34b93c21716a0583f98/src/auto-reply/reply/abort-primitives.ts#L12-L18)
- [abort.ts](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/fead50a35107ed73cbb1f34b93c21716a0583f98/src/auto-reply/reply/abort.ts#L51-L84)
- [abort-cutoff.ts](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/fead50a35107ed73cbb1f34b93c21716a0583f98/src/auto-reply/reply/abort-cutoff.ts#L83-L96)
- [sessions/types.ts](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/fead50a35107ed73cbb1f34b93c21716a0583f98/src/config/sessions/types.ts#L448-L456)
- [dispatch-from-config.prepare-operation.ts](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/fead50a35107ed73cbb1f34b93c21716a0583f98/src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-from-config.prepare-operation.ts#L67)

## Validation

Zig 0.16.0, on this branch (based on current `main` = 5f1cade, plus the four follow-up commits):

```text
$ zig fmt --check src/
$ zig build test --summary all
Build Summary: 13/13 steps succeeded; 7505/7519 tests passed (14 skipped)
```

Twelve tests are added in total — five in the original commit and seven across the follow-ups:

- `routeInbound interrupts a busy session for /stop instead of dropping`: a `/stop` for a session whose queue mode is `off` still reaches the busy session and raises the interrupt flag; a non-stop message in the same state is still dropped without interrupt.
- `dispatcher interrupts a busy session for /stop before enqueue`: a `/stop` handled at dispatch time raises the running session's flag and is consumed; a normal message is left for the queue; a `/stop` with no running turn is not consumed.
- `stdinWriteFailureIsInterrupt reports a stop, not a write error`: the interrupt flag wins over the write error.
- `Agent ends the turn with the interrupt reply when the stream is interrupted`.
- `Agent ends the turn with the interrupt reply when /stop lands during the vision retry`.
- `Agent exposes the interrupt flag to the blocking provider request`: a turn without a stream sink takes the blocking branch with the flag installed, so a stop can abort it.
- `Agent ends a blocking turn when /stop aborts the provider request`: a blocking request killed by the watcher (`error.CurlInterrupted`) ends the turn with the interrupt reply, no retry.
- `ReliableProvider surfaces a user stop without retrying or failing over`: a `CurlInterrupted` from the inner provider propagates as `error.Interrupted` after exactly one attempt.
- `curlStream stops reading buffered deltas when the interrupt flag is raised`: a local SSE server emits a bounded stream; once the flag is raised the read loop stops after the first delta instead of draining what curl already buffered.
- `publishOutboundTimeout reports Timeout instead of blocking on a full queue`.
- `publishStreamingChunk drops a preview instead of blocking on a full outbound queue`: a full outbound queue drops the preview, the chunk is not enqueued and the call returns at once.
- `telegram /stop does not clobber the running turn's live draft`: a `/stop` for a busy session sets the interrupt flag and leaves the running turn's draft id and buffer untouched.

The five follow-up behaviour-regression tests (the A/B/D fixes: the whole-call interrupt flag and blocking-stop handling, the reliable-provider stop propagation, the `curlStream` read-loop check, and the Telegram route-before-draft reorder) were confirmed to fail against the pre-port code (their production fix reverted, the tests kept):

```text
$ zig build test --summary all   # A/B/D production fixes reverted (C kept, see below)
Build Summary: 11/13 steps succeeded (1 failed); 7500/7519 tests passed (14 skipped, 5 failed)
  agent.root.test.Agent exposes the interrupt flag to the blocking provider request...FAIL (TestUnexpectedResult)
  agent.root.test.Agent ends a blocking turn when /stop aborts the provider request...FAIL (TestUnexpectedResult)
  providers.reliable.test.ReliableProvider surfaces a user stop without retrying or failing over...expected error.Interrupted, found error.AllProvidersFailed
  providers.sse.test.curlStream stops reading buffered deltas when the interrupt flag is raised...FAIL (TestUnexpectedResult)
  channel_loop.test.telegram /stop does not clobber the running turn's live draft...expected 2, found 3
```

The two C tests are new-API/new-behaviour coverage rather than regressions of existing code, so they are not in the failure block above:

- `publishOutboundTimeout reports Timeout instead of blocking on a full queue` exercises the brand-new `Bus.publishOutboundTimeout`, which does not exist on the pre-port base, so it cannot fail against pre-port code (the revert run keeps C, since reverting it removes the API the test compiles against).
- `publishStreamingChunk drops a preview instead of blocking on a full outbound queue` cannot report a failure against the pre-port code either: with the blocking `publishOutbound` it parks on the full queue and never returns, so the run stalls at that test rather than failing — which is exactly the bug it guards.

Trial-merged onto `main` + #971 (native tool calls while streaming): the only conflict is the test region of `src/agent/root.zig`, where both PRs append tests at the same anchor; it resolves by keeping both. The suite passes:

```text
$ zig fmt --check src/
$ zig build test --summary all
Build Summary: 13/13 steps succeeded; 7513/7527 tests passed (14 skipped)
```

## Notes

- Changes `src/session.zig`, `src/daemon.zig`, `src/http_util.zig`, `src/providers/sse.zig`, `src/providers/compatible.zig`, `src/providers/reliable.zig`, `src/providers/gemini.zig`, `src/providers/openai_codex.zig`, `src/bus.zig`, `src/channel_loop.zig` and `src/agent/root.zig`. No config, API or behaviour change outside stop handling.
- Independent of #987 (loop hygiene): #987 reduces how often a turn loops without making progress, but gives the user no way to stop a turn that is already running; this is that escape hatch. #987 does not touch `/stop`, the inbound dispatcher or the provider stream.
- The dispatcher fast-path only consumes a stop when a turn is actually in flight (`requestTurnInterrupt` reports `requested`); otherwise the message routes normally and the user gets the usual reply.
- Combines with #971: #971 is provider/SSE tool-call plumbing, this is interrupt plumbing; trial-merging produces no non-test conflicts.
- Slack streamed-delta throttling and the "drop a stopped turn's queued chunks" cancel marker live in #1058, not here.

prs.title: fix(providers): discard tool calls from truncated responses and cap the batch
prs.body:
Tracked in #1066.

## Summary

When a model hits its output-token budget it stops with `finish_reason: "length"` (OpenAI/OpenRouter), `stop_reason: "max_tokens"` (Anthropic), `finishReason: "MAX_TOKENS"` (Gemini) or `status: "incomplete"` (Responses API). The text it produced is a truncated prefix, but nullclaw parsed `<tool_call>` markup out of that prefix and executed it. A cut argument object could be run as-is (for example a truncated shell command), and a batch was executed without any bound on its size. This change makes a truncated response's tool calls inert and caps a batch.

Providers now carry a `truncated` flag and set it from the terminal reason:

- `ChatResponse` and `StreamChatResult` gain `truncated: bool = false`, and `emitChatResponseAsStream` propagates it.
- `openai.zig`/`openrouter.zig` set it from `finish_reason == "length"`, `anthropic.zig` from `stop_reason == "max_tokens"`, `gemini.zig` from `finishReason == "MAX_TOKENS"` (and its recovered-stream finalizer), and `compatible.zig` from a Responses `status == "incomplete"`.
- `sse.zig` detects a `finish_reason: "length"` in the stream itself (`sseLineReportsLengthFinish`), flags the finalized result, and flags the salvage paths (wait failure, nonzero exit, abnormal termination) as truncated.

The agent refuses tool calls from a truncated response and bounds a batch:

- After a streamed or blocking response is parsed, if it is `truncated` the parsed tool calls are discarded and the turn ends with `TRUNCATED_RESPONSE_NOTICE` instead of executing them.
- A batch larger than `MAX_TOOL_CALLS_PER_BATCH` (24) is rejected as a whole, with a `Rejected a tool-call batch` notice, without executing anything and without a second provider iteration. The batch cap bounds the damage a single response can do; the truncated guard covers the case where the model was cut off mid-batch.

The `truncated` field is new: current `main` has no such plumbing (`ChatResponse.truncated`, `StreamChatResult.truncated`, `choiceReportsLengthFinish` and the `emitChatResponseAsStream` propagation are all added here).

The output cap is now delivered in the field a reasoning gateway honours:

- `src/providers/helpers.zig`: `appendGenerationFields` sends the resolved output cap as `max_completion_tokens` when a reasoning effort is active (`reasoningEffortActive`) or the model name marks an OpenAI-compatible reasoning endpoint that `isReasoningModel` does not recognise (`isReasoningEndpointModel`: `reason`/`think`/`k2`), and as `max_tokens` otherwise. A gateway that is not one of OpenAI's own model ids (K2, DeepSeek-R1, `…-thinking`) ignores `max_tokens` and honours only `max_completion_tokens`, so before this the cap never applied and a degenerate loop ran to the gateway's hard output ceiling — the same runaway the truncated guard catches, but unbounded.
- The cap value is unchanged: it is the top-level `max_tokens` override, resolved per model by `max_tokens.zig`. That override was undocumented; it is now described in `docs/en/configuration.md` and `docs/zh/configuration.md`.

### Related upstream work

- #971 (open) "native tool calls during SSE streaming" refuses to execute a tool call salvaged from a stream that was *cut* (curl timeout, nonzero exit, abnormal termination). This PR covers the case #971 does not: a stream that ended *cleanly* because the model reached its token limit (`finish_reason: "length"`), where the SSE stream is complete and #971's recovery-path guard never fires. It also adds the batch cap, which #971 does not have. The two compose: this PR's `truncated` flag is set on the same recovery paths #971 already marks untrusted, so a trial-merge keeps both. #971's `finalizeStreamResultWithToolCalls(..., tool_calls_trusted)` and this PR's `finalizeRecoveredStreamResult` are resolved so the recovery paths keep #971's untrusted-tool-call semantics and this PR's `truncated` flag.
- #965 (closed) "structured streaming tool-call support for SSE parser" was the earlier SSE tool-call proposal that #971 superseded.
- #572 (merged) "prevent redundant tool execution via turn-scoped deduplication" is the dedup the `Agent executes a repeated text tool call once per batch` test exercises.
- #228 (closed) "Security: Nullclaw leaks tool calls to chat" and #407/#408 (closed, tool-name/JSON parsing) are earlier tool-call-parsing issues.
- Prior-art search (open and closed PRs, issues, all open PR titles) found no PR that flags a `length`/`max_tokens` response as truncated across providers, that caps a tool-call batch, or that routes the output cap to `max_completion_tokens` for a reasoning endpoint `isReasoningModel` does not know.

### OpenClaw reference

OpenClaw treats a `length` stop as an incomplete turn and does not expect a post-tool continuation from it: `isIncompleteTerminalAssistantTurn` in `incomplete-turn-classification.ts` returns true for a `length` stop only when there is no terminal output and no visible text (a `toolUse` stop is the one that expects a continuation), and `terminal-resolution.ts` labels a `length` stop with partial text (`isTruncatedPartialReply`) rather than treating the turn as complete. Tool execution is bounded by a per-invocation budget: `createAgentToolExecutionBudget` in `agent-tool-source-execution-guard.ts` counts admitted calls and aborts when `toolCalls >= maxToolCalls`. For the cap field, OpenClaw's `maxTokensField` defaults to `max_completion_tokens` for OpenAI-compatible endpoints, which is the field the cap is routed to here.

- [incomplete-turn-classification.ts](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/fead50a35107ed73cbb1f34b93c21716a0583f98/src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/incomplete-turn-classification.ts#L160-L175)
- [terminal-resolution.ts](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/fead50a35107ed73cbb1f34b93c21716a0583f98/src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/terminal-resolution.ts#L585-L588)
- [agent-tool-source-execution-guard.ts](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/fead50a35107ed73cbb1f34b93c21716a0583f98/src/agents/agent-tool-source-execution-guard.ts#L18-L62)

## Validation

Zig 0.16.0, on this branch (based on current `main` = 5f1cade):

```text

$ zig build test --summary all
Build Summary: 13/13 steps succeeded; 7516/7530 tests passed (14 skipped)
```

- Provider parsers: `parseNativeResponse flags stop_reason=max_tokens as truncated` / `... leaves truncated false on end_turn` (Anthropic), `parseNativeResponse flags finish_reason=length as truncated` / `... leaves truncated false on a natural stop` (OpenAI, OpenRouter, compatible), `parseChatResponse flags finishReason=MAX_TOKENS as truncated` / `... leaves truncated false on a STOP finish` (Gemini), `parseResponsesResponse flags status=incomplete as truncated` / `... leaves truncated false on a completed response`, `finalizeRecoveredGeminiStreamResult flags a cut stream as truncated`.
- SSE: `sseLineReportsLengthFinish detects a max_tokens finish`, `sseLineReportsLengthFinish finds finish_reason past 16 KB`, `finalizeRecoveredStreamResult flags a cut stream as truncated`, `emitChatResponseAsStream propagates the truncated flag`.
- Agent: `Agent discards tool calls from a truncated provider response`, `Agent rejects an oversized tool-call batch`, `Agent executes a repeated text tool call once per batch`.
- Output cap (`src/providers/helpers.zig`): `appendGenerationFields uses max_completion_tokens for an active reasoning effort`, `appendGenerationFields keeps max_tokens for a plain model without an effort`, `appendGenerationFields caps a reasoning endpoint even without an effort`. The first and third fail pre-fix — with the cap logic reverted but the tests kept, they fail at the `max_completion_tokens` assertion (`error.TestUnexpectedResult`) because pre-fix a `k2` request emitted the cap as `max_tokens`; the second is a characterization of the untouched plain-model path. prs.title: fix(providers): send /think levels to OpenAI-compatible models and add max
prs.body:
> Tracking: #1066

> Stacked on #1064 (it reuses that PR's retry path in `compatible.zig`). Only the last commit is new; I will rebase once #1064 is merged or dropped.

## Summary

`/think` and the config `reasoning_effort` only reach OpenAI reasoning models. `appendGenerationFields` drops the field for every model `isReasoningModel` does not recognise (`gpt-5*`, `o1`, `o3`, `o4-mini`, `codex-mini`). So on DeepSeek, Kimi, K2 and other OpenAI-compatible models behind the compatible provider, the chosen level is silently ignored. Those endpoints take the same top-level `reasoning_effort` field.

I confirmed this from the gateway side: none of the requests nullclaw sent carried `reasoning_effort`, whatever `/think` was set to.

Changes:

- **Send the level to OpenAI-compatible models.** The compatible provider now adds `reasoning_effort` for models outside `isReasoningModel`. `minimal` maps to `low`; `xhigh` and `max` pass through. Providers that already map reasoning_effort to their own field are unchanged and do not get the extra field:
  - GLM `thinking`
  - Qwen `enable_thinking`
  - MiniMax `reasoning_split`
  - vLLM `chat_template_kwargs`
- **Learn per-model limits from rejections.** Measured against the endpoints:
  - DeepSeek accepts `low`/`high`/`xhigh`/`max`.
  - IFM K2 rejects `xhigh`/`max` with `400 Invalid value for 'reasoning_effort'`.

  On that error the provider records a limit for that model and resends. A level above `high` is lowered to `high`. If `high` is rejected too, the field is dropped for that model. Limits are kept per model, because one provider entry often serves models with different ranges, so K2's rejection does not lower DeepSeek's level.
- **Add `max`.** `/think` and config `reasoning_effort` accept `max`. OpenAI reasoning models, Gemini and the Codex provider map it like `xhigh`. The Codex provider previously sent `xhigh` verbatim, which its backend rejects; it now normalizes the same way as the other OpenAI paths.

This matches how OpenClaw handles OpenAI-compatible reasoning effort: its thinking ladder includes `xhigh` and `max`, and it clamps to `high` for models that only support the standard levels.

## Validation

Zig 0.16.0, on this branch:

```text
$ zig fmt --check src/
$ zig build test --summary all
Build Summary: 13/13 steps succeeded; 7498/7512 tests passed (14 skipped)
```

New tests:
- the field is sent to non-OpenAI models with the right mapping
- it is absent without a level
- OpenAI models still get exactly one normalized field
- providers with a native thinking field get no extra field, on both the streaming and non-streaming builders
- per-model limit learning: lower to `high`, then drop; another model behind the same provider keeps its level; unrelated errors do not retry

The two tests that guard the bugs fixed here (the level being dropped on non-OpenAI models, and an endpoint rejecting a level above `high`) carry a `// Regression:` comment citing the failure they guard against, per `AGENTS.md` section 8.1.

Running against live endpoints through an OpenAI-style gateway, with `/think max`:
- DeepSeek received `reasoning_effort: "max"`.
- K2 logged `rejected reasoning_effort=max for k2; resending with high`, and the retry succeeded with `high`.

## Notes

- Only changes behaviour when a reasoning level is set. With no `/think` and no config `reasoning_effort`, request bodies are unchanged.
- Files: `src/providers/{compatible,helpers,openai_codex}.zig`, `src/agent/commands.zig`, `src/config_parse.zig`.

prs.title: fix(providers): route configured providers by explicit prefix
prs.body:
> Tracking: #1066

# PR title

fix(providers): route configured providers by explicit prefix

# Branch

fix/route-providers-by-prefix

# PR body

## What changed

An explicit `provider/model` model reference previously resolved only for the primary provider and for providers listed in `reliability.fallback_providers`. A provider that is configured under `models.providers` but is not a fallback target was never registered as a routing target, so `/model <provider-alias>/<model-id>` was unusable for it. This PR makes every configured provider reachable by its explicit prefix, without adding it to the failover chain.

Two files:

- `src/providers/reliable.zig`: new `routable` field on `ReliableProvider` (defaults to `&.{}`, so the struct stays backward compatible), a `withRoutable()` builder next to the existing `withExtras()` / `withModelFallbacks()`, and the explicit-prefix matching extracted into a shared `matchExplicitProviders()` helper that is applied to `extras` and to `routable` with the same longest-prefix accounting. The exact-provider-name branch of `resolveProviderTarget()` consults `routable` (lookup order: `extras`, then `routable`, then the primary provider). `deinit()` and `warmup()` now cover the new slice.
- `src/providers/runtime_bundle.zig`: new `collectRoutableProviderNames()` collects every provider configured under `models.providers` except the default provider (already the primary) and providers already covered by `reliability.fallback_providers` (name comparison via `provider_names.providerNamesMatch`, duplicates skipped). The extra-slot arrays are sized as `reliability.fallback_providers.len + rotating_key_count + routable.len`, and the single entry array is split back into two slices at wiring time: `entries[0..failover_entry_count]` goes to `withExtras()`, `entries[failover_entry_count..]` goes to `withRoutable()`. When the inner provider is the provider router, no routable entries are built, since the router already resolves explicit refs against the same provider set.

## Why it changed

Concrete failure, all names placeholders:

1. `models.providers` contains the default provider `<primary-provider>` and a second provider `<provider-alias>` whose `base_url` points at a gateway that serves `<model-id>`.
2. `reliability.fallback_providers` is empty, or lists a different provider. The user runs `/model <provider-alias>/<model-id>`.
3. `RuntimeProviderBundle.init()` registered only `reliability.fallback_providers` (plus rotated keys) as `ReliableProvider` extras, so `<provider-alias>` had no entry anywhere in the wrapper.
4. `resolveProviderTarget()` found no explicit-prefix match, fell through to the bare-model path, stripped the `<provider-alias>/` prefix, and sent `<model-id>` to the primary provider.
5. `<primary-provider>` does not serve `<model-id>` and rejects the request with `Model <model-id> is not allowed`.

The prefix was parsed correctly the whole time. The only defect was that the provider it named was never registered as a routable target, which also explains why the workaround was to add the provider to `reliability.fallback_providers` even when it was not wanted as a failover target.

## Routing and failover stay separate

This is the part worth reviewing closely. `routable` is not a second failover chain:

- `extras` still contains exactly `reliability.fallback_providers` plus rotated keys, in configured order. Nothing was added to it, and `withExtras()` receives the same bounds as before (`entries[0..failover_entry_count]`).
- `routable` entries are consulted only in the explicit-prefix paths: longest-prefix matching against both the configured entry name and the provider runtime name, plus the exact `provider/model` name lookup in `resolveProviderTarget()`. A bare model never consults them.
- A bare model (`<model-id>` with no prefix) therefore keeps its existing behavior: it goes to the primary provider, and on failure it fails over through the configured `fallback_providers` only. A configured-but-not-fallback provider is never used as a failover target.
- The regression test `ReliableProvider keeps failover limited to extras` pins this: the primary fails, the configured fallback serves the request, and the routable-only provider is asserted to have received zero calls.

## Validation

Run locally on the PR head `ffec4598` with Zig 0.16.0:

- `zig fmt --check src/` (what `.githooks/pre-commit` runs) — clean, no output.
- `zig build test --summary all` (required for code changes) — `Build Summary: 13/13 steps succeeded; 7497/7511 tests passed (14 skipped)`, 0 failures, 0 leaks.
- `zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseSmall` — not run; this is not a release-sensitive change.

Green CI on the fix commit `59564ec2`, all three matrix jobs success — https://github.com/nullclaw/nullclaw/actions/runs/38655339567. The branch head adds a comment-only follow-up (`ffec4598`), so these results carry over.

- `zig / linux-x86_64` — success
- `zig / macos-aarch64` — success
- `zig / windows-x86_64` — success

Tests added here (4 new):

- `ReliableProvider routes an explicit prefix to a non-failover provider` (new, `reliable.zig`): the prefixed reference reaches the routable provider, that provider receives the bare model id, and the primary is not called.
- `ReliableProvider keeps failover limited to extras` (new, `reliable.zig`): bare-model failover behavior is unchanged.
- `RuntimeProviderBundle makes non-fallback configured providers routable` (new, `runtime_bundle.zig`): for a config whose second provider is not a fallback target, `extras.len == 0` and `routable.len == 1`.
- `RuntimeProviderBundle keeps fallback providers in the failover chain` (new, `runtime_bundle.zig`): the fallback target stays in `extras` while the other configured provider lands in `routable`.

Each new test carries a comment naming the regression it guards, per `AGENTS.md` 8.1.

## Notes

- No config surface change: no new keys, no changed defaults, no new CLI flags. The only new state is internal (`routable`), derived from the existing `models.providers` and `reliability.fallback_providers`.
- Backward compatible: existing configurations keep identical behavior for bare models and for failover. The only behavior change is that an explicit `provider/model` reference to a configured provider now resolves instead of being stripped and rejected by the primary provider.
- Rollback: `git revert` of the squash commit. No migration, no persisted state, nothing written to disk.
- Docs: this restores behavior that `docs/en/commands.md` already documents (`/model <provider/model>` pins the session to that model). No config key or flag text changes, so no doc edit is strictly required; if maintainers want it explicit, the clarification belongs in that `/model` bullet.
- Ownership: routable entries are appended to the same `reliable_entries` / `extra_holders` arrays the bundle already owns and frees, so deinit stays in one place. The collected name slice borrows from `cfg.providers`, which outlives the bundle, and is freed by `init()` once the entries are built.
- Risk tier: medium per `AGENTS.md` 5 (`src/providers/**` behavior change, no boundary or security impact).

prs.title: fix(telegram): keep the live draft owned by the running turn
prs.body:
Tracked in #1066.

## Summary

Telegram's per-chat live-draft slot (`draft_buffers`) had no notion of turn ownership. Every inbound message ran `startTypingTurn` -> `beginDraftTurn` -> `beginDraftStateLocked`, which cleared the chat's draft buffer and rotated its `draft_id`, and the deferred `finishDraftTurn` then deleted the slot. When a second message (or an interactive callback) was handled while a turn was still generating, it reset or deleted the draft that the running turn's `StreamCtx` still held, so every later streamed reasoning chunk hit the `draft_id` mismatch guard in `sendDraftChunkForTurn` and was silently dropped. The user was left with only the "Interim result is still being prepared." heartbeat.

This change makes the draft owned by the turn that began it:

- `DraftState` gains an `active` flag, set when a turn claims the draft.
- `beginDraftTurn` refuses to clobber an active draft (returns 0), so a second caller starts no draft and cannot orphan the running one.
- `startTypingTurn` claims the draft before touching the typing loop and returns a `TypingTurn{started, draft_id}`; when it cannot claim a draft it leaves the owner (and its typing indicator) untouched.
- `startTyping`, the generic `Channel` entry point the daemon/webhook inbound indicator uses, now starts only the typing loop. It must not claim a draft, because that path creates and releases the draft through `sendEvent` chunk/final rather than through `finishDraftTurn`.
- `processTelegramMessage` and `handleTelegramInteractiveCallback` consult the inbound router before starting the typing/draft turn, so an injected or dropped message never resets the running turn's draft.

The daemon path creates the draft lazily through `sendEvent(.chunk)` and releases it on every turn-final delivery, including the inline-choices (`sendRich`) and replace_message (`editMessage`) paths that bypass `sendEvent(.final)`, so the next turn starts from a clean, empty draft. `finishDraftTurn` already clears only its own draft id, and a queued message that later runs its own turn gets a fresh draft because the previous turn's slot was already removed.

### Related upstream work

- #943 added the typing/draft dance to `handleTelegramInteractiveCallback` (mirroring `processTelegramMessage`), closing #942. That is what made a button press start a second draft turn, so this fix also covers the callback path.
- #845, #846 and #855 added the inbound router and mid-turn injection (#832). Once a message can be folded into the running turn, it still went through the full `startTypingTurn` dance first; this change routes before the dance so an injected/dropped message leaves the running draft alone.
- Prior-art search (open and closed PRs, issues, all open PR titles) found no existing PR for draft ownership.

### OpenClaw reference

OpenClaw ties the draft stream to the turn. In `extensions/telegram/src/draft-stream.ts` a draft stream is created per run and finalized at teardown. In `extensions/telegram/src/bot-message-dispatch-draft.ts` the draft lane carries a `finalized` flag, and a new message either repositions the still-active lane (`repositionLaneForNewMessage`) or rotates an already-finalized one (`rotateLaneForNewMessage`), so an active stream is never cleared or deleted mid-turn; `retireAnswerLane` finalizes at turn end. `docs/concepts/queue.md` records that a mid-run prompt defaults to `steer` (injected into the active runtime, not a second run) and that typing indicators still fire immediately on enqueue.

- [draft-stream.ts](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/fead50a35107ed73cbb1f34b93c21716a0583f98/extensions/telegram/src/draft-stream.ts)
- [bot-message-dispatch-draft.ts](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/fead50a35107ed73cbb1f34b93c21716a0583f98/extensions/telegram/src/bot-message-dispatch-draft.ts#L143-L245)
- [queue.md](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/fead50a35107ed73cbb1f34b93c21716a0583f98/docs/concepts/queue.md)

## Validation

Zig 0.16.0, on this branch (rebased on current `main`):

```text
$ zig fmt --check src/
$ zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseSmall
$ zig build test --summary all
Build Summary: 13/13 steps succeeded; 7497/7511 tests passed (14 skipped)
```

Four tests are added in `src/channels/telegram.zig`:

- `startTypingTurn refuses to clobber a draft owned by a running turn`: a second `startTypingTurn` mid-turn reports no draft, leaves the owner's `draft_id` and buffer intact, and the owner's later chunks still land; after the owner finishes, the next turn gets a fresh draft.
- `startTyping (daemon indicator) does not claim the live draft`.
- `daemon turn ending with inline choices releases the live draft`: a daemon turn creates the draft through `sendEvent(.chunk)` and releases it when it finalizes through `sendRich`; a later polling turn can claim a fresh draft.
- `replace_message edit releases the live draft`: `editMessage` releases the draft even when the edit itself fails before any network call.

Trial-merged onto `main` + #971 (native tool calls while streaming): merges cleanly, no conflicts, and both checks pass:

```text
$ zig fmt --check src/
$ zig build test --summary all
Build Summary: 13/13 steps succeeded; 7512/7526 tests passed (14 skipped)
```

## Notes

- Independent of #1062 (render live drafts with HTML parse mode). #1062 changes how the draft body is rendered and sent; this changes who owns the draft slot. They touch different hunks of `src/channels/telegram.zig` and can land in either order. They are not combined here.
- Combines with #971 (native tool calls while streaming): #971 is in the provider/SSE layer, this is in the channel typing/draft layer, and they do not overlap. Trial-merging this branch onto `main` + #971 produces no conflicts and the suite passes (result above).
- Only `src/channel_loop.zig`, `src/channels/telegram.zig` and `src/channels/telegram_draft_presenter.zig` change. No config, API, or behaviour change outside Telegram draft ownership.

prs.title: fix(providers): resend assistant history with reasoning_content when required
prs.body:
> Tracking: #1066

## Summary

Some OpenAI-compatible endpoints require a thinking field on every assistant message of a multi-turn request. IFM's K2 models (reached here through an OpenAI-style gateway) answer with:

```text
400 Add a supported thinking field to each assistant message in the multi-turn conversation history.
```

nullclaw never sends one. As soon as a session has one assistant turn, every later request in it fails, and the only way out for the user is `/new`.

Two problems made this hard to see:

1. **No thinking field.** `ChatMessage` gets an optional `reasoning_content` that the compatible serializer emits on assistant messages. When the endpoint returns this specific error, the provider remembers it and resends the request once with an empty `reasoning_content` on every assistant message. Later requests include it directly, so existing sessions recover without `/new`. I checked against the endpoint: an empty string is accepted, and so is `reasoning`. Other endpoints are unaffected because the field is only added after this rejection.
2. **The error text was dropped on the streaming path.** `sse.curlStream` classified a JSON error body but never recorded it, so channels showed only `An error occurred. Try again or /new for a fresh session.` and the log only `error.ApiError`. It is now recorded with `setLastApiErrorDetail` like the non-streaming path, so the real reason reaches the user and the log.

## Validation

Zig 0.16.0, on this branch (based on current `main`), at the current head:

```text
$ zig fmt --check src/
$ zig build test --summary all
Build Summary: 13/13 steps succeeded; 7495/7509 tests passed (14 skipped)
```

New tests:
- `reasoning_content` is serialized on an assistant message only when set.
- Only the missing-thinking-field `ApiError` triggers the resend. A rate-limit message or a different error does not. The resend happens once, and afterwards only assistant messages get the field.

Both new tests carry a `// Regression:` comment citing the IFM K2 rejection they guard against, per `AGENTS.md` section 8.1.

## Notes

- Only `src/providers/{compatible,root,sse}.zig` change. No config change.
- The `sse.zig` change is logging-only and only runs with a live child and a JSON error body, so it has no unit test; a comment near the change records why, per `AGENTS.md` section 8.1. The helpers it calls (`summarizeKnownApiError`, `setLastApiErrorDetail`) keep their own tests.
- The history does not keep reasoning text, so the resent field is empty. Endpoints that need the actual reasoning back (rather than the field's presence) would need history to store it. That is a larger change and out of scope here.

prs.title: feat(security): per-agent autonomy for named agents
prs.body:
> Tracking: #1066

## Summary

Every named agent currently runs under the global `autonomy` policy. `SessionManager` builds each agent runtime's tools from `config.autonomy` and shares one global `SecurityPolicy`, so a guest agent bound to a single chat peer through `bindings` gets exactly the same shell and file permissions as the main agent. With a `full` or `yolo` main agent, any bound peer can run arbitrary shell commands and read `config.json` (provider keys, channel tokens).

This adds an optional `autonomy` object to `agents.list[]` entries:

```json
{
  "agents": {
    "list": [
      { "id": "guest", "provider": "openrouter", "model": "...", "workspace_path": "agents/guest",
        "autonomy": { "level": "read_only" } }
    ]
  }
}
```

- It accepts the same keys as the top-level `autonomy` block and **replaces** the global one for that agent. Omitted keys fall back to the secure `AutonomyConfig` defaults instead of inheriting the global (possibly `yolo`) values. An unknown `level` is rejected at config load.
- An agent with its own autonomy always gets a dedicated runtime that owns its own `SecurityPolicy` and `RateTracker`, scoped to its own workspace. `makeAgentConfig` also carries the agent's autonomy, so `Agent.fromConfigWithProfile` derives `exec_security`, `allowed_paths` and `multimodal_unrestricted` from it.
- `nullclaw agent --agent <name>` applies the same policy.
- Agents without an `autonomy` block behave exactly as before.

### What is closed for an agent with its own autonomy

A stricter policy is only meaningful if the agent cannot reach the global policy or the host through another door, so these are closed too:

- **Tools that act under the global policy or outside the workspace are withheld:** `spawn` (subagents run under the global config), `schedule` (cron shell jobs use the scheduler's global policy), `delegate` (runs any configured agent's provider with the operator's key), MCP tools (child processes that never consult the policy), `git` (writes regardless of `read_only`), `screenshot`, `image_info` (opens any absolute path).
- **Global config surface:** `/config` and `/export` are refused, `/capabilities` and the `/model` menu no longer read the shared `config.json`, `/model` does not persist the global default, and Telegram `/bind` is refused for a peer routed to such an agent (otherwise `/bind clear` escapes back to the default agent).
- **Attachments:** legacy `[DOCUMENT:]`/`[FILE:]`/`[IMAGE:]` markers in the reply are filtered at the session boundary. A local target must resolve (realpath) inside the agent's workspace or its own `allowed_paths`. Previously any absolute path was uploaded, even under `read_only`, because this does not go through a tool call. Inbound `[IMAGE:/tmp/...]` reads of the platform temp dir are refused as well.
- **Shell confinement (`supervised`/`full`):** arguments that name a path outside the workspace (absolute, `..`, `~`) are rejected. Commands are restricted to a strict byte set (letters, digits, spaces, `;`, `|`, `&&`, `||`, `-_./,:=+@%^`), so quotes, redirections, escapes, `$` expansion and globs, which the shell would rewrite after the check, are refused. Package-manager run verbs and script-running git subcommands are refused, as are `find` exec/write predicates.

The shell confinement is a best-effort argument check, not a filesystem jail. The docs (en + zh) say so explicitly and recommend `"level": "read_only"` for untrusted guests, which disables all tool calls.

### Two latent fixes found while testing

- An unknown autonomy level is rejected before `parseJson` writes any field, so `Config.load` no longer keeps a half-parsed config.
- `Config.save` frees each serialized agent `api_key` exactly once: the cleanup defer is registered before the serialization loop, so a failure inside the loop or after it neither double-frees nor leaks the keys.

## Validation

Zig 0.16.0, on this branch (rebased on current `main`):

```text
$ zig fmt --check src/
$ zig build test --summary all
Build Summary: 13/13 steps succeeded; 7518/7532 tests passed (14 skipped)
```

New tests cover the config parse/reject paths, the dedicated runtime and policy, withheld tools, `/config`, `/export` and `/bind` refusal, attachment filtering, the temp-dir image refusal, and the shell confinement (including `cat ''/etc/passwd`, `cat </etc/passwd`, `cat \/etc/passwd`, `cat $IFS/etc/passwd`, `find . -fprint x`). The `Config.save` agent `api_key` cleanup has a `checkAllAllocationFailures` regression test that fails every allocation point of a save with two keyed agents and asserts each key is freed exactly once.

Also running on a live gateway with a `yolo` main agent and a `read_only` guest bound to one peer: the main agent's shell is unrestricted, the guest's shell calls return `Action blocked: agent is in read-only mode`, and `nullclaw doctor` is clean.

## Notes

- This is large because each closed door needed its own change. Happy to split it (config + dedicated runtime first, then withheld tools, then attachments/slash commands, then shell confinement) if that is easier to review.
- No behaviour change for configs without `agents.list[].autonomy`.
- The two latent fixes above were found while building this: the half-parse guard because the feature makes `autonomy.level` a user-typed value in two places, and the `Config.save` cleanup while extending the serialized agent entry. Both are small, independent of the feature's behaviour, and covered by regression tests; happy to split them into their own PR if you prefer.

prs.title: feat(telegram): render live drafts with HTML parse mode
prs.body:
> Tracking: #1066

## Summary

Telegram live drafts are sent through `sendMessageDraft` as plain text, while the finalized reply goes through `markdownToTelegramHtml` and is sent with `parse_mode: "HTML"`. Anything formatted in the streaming draft (quoted reasoning, bold, inline code, lists) therefore shows up as raw Markdown until the final message replaces the draft, and the formatting appears to "jump" at the end of every turn.

This change renders the draft the same way the final message is rendered:

- `sendDraft` converts the preview text with the existing `markdownToTelegramHtml` and sends it with `parse_mode: "HTML"`. `sendMessageDraft` accepts `parse_mode` like `sendMessage` does.
- The body construction moves into a small `buildDraftBody` helper so the same request can be sent with or without `parse_mode`, and the retry decision moves into `draftNeedsPlainTextFallback`.
- A draft is the tail of a message that is still being generated, so it can end inside markup that Telegram rejects. When Telegram answers with `can't parse entities`, the same draft is resent as plain text, which is always accepted. Other errors keep going through the existing handling (rate limits, unsupported peer, message too long).
- If the conversion itself fails, the plain text is sent as before.

The 4096-character limit is unaffected in practice: `buildTransportText` caps the draft source at 3000 bytes, and the "message too long" handling still applies if an HTML expansion ever exceeds the limit.

## Validation

Run locally with Zig 0.16.0:

```text
$ zig fmt --check src/
$ zig build test --summary all
Build Summary: 13/13 steps succeeded; 7497/7511 tests passed (14 skipped)
```

The fallback path is covered by unit tests added in this PR: `buildDraftBody` with and without `parse_mode` (including `message_thread_id`), and `draftNeedsPlainTextFallback` for the parse-entity error, a plain-text attempt, the phrase without a Telegram error object, and an unrelated API error.

Manually verified on a live Telegram bot: with `/reasoning stream`, the streamed reasoning renders as a quote block and formatting in the in-progress answer renders while streaming; the final message is unchanged.

## Notes

- Only `src/channels/telegram.zig` changes. No config, API, or behavior change outside draft rendering.
- Tests: the network send path is still stubbed out (`sendDraft` returns early under `builtin.is_test`), so the request body and the fallback decision were extracted into pure functions (`buildDraftBody`, `draftNeedsPlainTextFallback`) and covered by unit tests in `src/channels/telegram.zig`.

prs.title: feat(slack): show the task lifecycle as reactions
prs.body:
> Tracking: #1066

# feat(slack): show the task lifecycle as reactions

**Branch:** `feat/slack-status-reactions`
**Base:** `main`
**Title:** `feat(slack): show the task lifecycle as reactions`

## What changed

Adds Slack status reactions: the message that triggers a turn gets a reaction that
follows the task through `accepted`, `running`, and `done` or `failed`.

```
 docs/en/configuration.md  |  25 ++++
 docs/zh/configuration.md  |  20 +++
 src/channels/root.zig     |  27 +++++
 src/channels/slack.zig    | 248 ++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++
 src/channels/telegram.zig |  10 +-
 src/config.zig            |  43 +++++++
 src/config_types.zig      |  16 +++
 src/daemon.zig            |  42 ++++++-
 8 files changed, 424 insertions(+), 7 deletions(-)
```

- `src/channels/root.zig`: new `Channel.TaskReaction` enum (`accepted`, `running`,
  `done`, `failed`), new `TaskReactionUpdate` payload, and a new vtable field
  `setTaskReaction` defaulting to `defaultSetTaskReaction`, which returns
  `error.NotSupported`. The default lets the daemon name a lifecycle state on any
  channel without every existing channel file changing.
- `src/channels/slack.zig`: `SlackChannel.setTaskReaction` plus the pure
  `planTaskReaction` transition table, the target parser `slackChannelIdOf`, the
  `reactions.add` / `reactions.remove` request builder, and the vtable wiring
  (`vtableSetTaskReaction`). The account latches `reactions_disabled` on an auth
  failure.
- `src/channels/telegram.zig`: `pub const TaskReaction` becomes an alias for
  `root.Channel.TaskReaction`. No other Telegram change.
- `src/config_types.zig`: `SlackReactionEmojisConfig` and the two new optional
  `SlackConfig` fields.
- `src/config.zig`: parsing tests for the defaults and for an explicit config.
- `src/daemon.zig`: `setInboundTaskReaction` helper, called from
  `processInboundMessage` on the accepted, running, and every terminal path.
- `docs/en/configuration.md`, `docs/zh/configuration.md`: the two new keys, a
  "Slack status reactions" section, and a config example, per the CONTRIBUTING
  rule that user-facing changes update docs in the same PR.

## Why it changed

`status_reactions` and `reaction_emojis` existed only under
`channels.telegram.accounts.<id>`, and the code that drives them is Telegram's
inherent `setTaskReaction`, which is called from the Telegram polling loop. Slack
does not run that loop: it receives events through its own socket/HTTP event
pipeline, so there was no place in the Slack path for the lifecycle to attach to,
and the same config keys would have been dead for Slack.

Copying the Telegram lifecycle into Slack would have forked the state machine into
a second implementation that can drift from the first. Instead the daemon names
the state and the channel keeps the mapping, which is the pattern AGENTS.md
prescribes: extension work implements vtable structs and registers them, it does
not add cross-cutting branches per channel.

## Design notes

### The vtable hook

`Channel.setTaskReaction(update: TaskReactionUpdate)` is a new function-pointer
field on `Channel.VTable`, following the same shape as the existing `setReaction`
and `markRead` hooks. The default implementation returns `error.NotSupported`, so:

- a channel that does not implement the hook is not a compile error and not a
  silent no-op either; the caller gets an explicit error it can ignore,
- the daemon can call the hook unconditionally and let the channel decide.

`setInboundTaskReaction` in `src/daemon.zig` swallows exactly `error.NotSupported`
and logs anything else at debug level. Telegram's vtable is not touched by this
change, so the hook is a no-op for Telegram and its polling-loop lifecycle keeps
running exactly as before.

`Channel.TaskReaction` is the shared vocabulary because the states themselves are
domain-neutral. `telegram.TaskReaction` becomes an alias for it rather than a
duplicate enum, so Telegram's existing call sites and tests keep compiling.

### Where the states are emitted

`processInboundMessage` emits the same sequence the Telegram loop uses, through
the `setInboundTaskReaction` helper:

| State | Emitted |
|---|---|
| `accepted` | after the routing decision returns something other than `.skip`, before the processing indicator |
| `running` | immediately before `processMessageStreaming` |
| `done` | on the draft-edit path and on the normal publish path, after the outbound event is published |
| `failed` | on the streaming error, the draft send failure, the publish failure, and the `makeOutbound` failure |

Every terminal path sets a final state, so a turn does not leave a stale
`accepted` or `running` reaction behind. The helper returns without calling the
channel when there is no message id to react to.

### Why the state to reaction mapping stays channel-local

The daemon passes a state name; each channel resolves it against its own config.
That split is deliberate:

- the value domain differs per channel. Telegram takes emoji characters
  (`TelegramReactionEmojisConfig` defaults to `👀 ⚡ 👍 💔`), Slack takes reaction
  short names (`eyes`, `hourglass_flowing_sand`, `white_check_mark`, `x`). The two
  are not interchangeable, which is why `SlackReactionEmojisConfig` is its own
  struct and only the enum is shared,
- the transport differs. Slack needs a remove-then-add plan, Telegram does not,
- the config type lives next to the channel config it parses, so a new channel
  adds a hook implementation without the daemon learning anything about reactions.

### Add, not replace

Slack reactions accumulate on a message. Adding `white_check_mark` after `eyes`
leaves both, so a transition has to remove the state it is leaving before adding
the state it is entering. `planTaskReaction` returns a `ReactionPlan` of up to two
removals and one add:

| New state | Supersedes | Default plan |
|---|---|---|
| `accepted` | none | add `eyes` |
| `running` | `accepted` | remove `eyes`, add `hourglass_flowing_sand` |
| `done` | `accepted`, `running` | remove `eyes`, remove `hourglass_flowing_sand`, add `white_check_mark` |
| `failed` | `accepted`, `running` | remove `eyes`, remove `hourglass_flowing_sand`, add `x` |

Two properties fall out of the same table:

- **Zero extra calls when two states share a name.** If the name being added
  equals a superseded state's name, that removal is skipped, so the reaction
  already on the message stays put. Setting `accepted` and `running` to
  `hourglass_flowing_sand` makes the `running` transition one add and zero
  removals.
- **An empty name withdraws the state.** `reactionEmoji` maps an empty string to
  null, which drops that state's add and still removes the superseded occurrence.
  With every name empty the plan is empty and no API call is made at all.

Duplicate removals are collapsed, so the plan never issues the same remove twice.

`planTaskReaction` is a pure function, which is what makes the transition table
testable without a network.

### Error handling

`already_reacted` and `no_reaction` are treated as success, so a retry or a
double transition is harmless. Any code matched by the existing
`SlackChannel.isAuthFailureCode` (which already covers `missing_scope`) latches
`reactions_disabled` and logs one warning per account; later turns skip the calls
entirely. Reaction failures never propagate: `setTaskReaction` is best-effort and
returns `void`, so a reaction problem cannot fail a turn.

## Config surface

Two optional keys on the Slack alias, mirroring Telegram's key names:

| Key | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `channels.slack.accounts.<alias>.status_reactions` | bool | `false` |
| `channels.slack.accounts.<alias>.reaction_emojis.accepted` | string | `eyes` |
| `channels.slack.accounts.<alias>.reaction_emojis.running` | string | `hourglass_flowing_sand` |
| `channels.slack.accounts.<alias>.reaction_emojis.done` | string | `white_check_mark` |
| `channels.slack.accounts.<alias>.reaction_emojis.failed` | string | `x` |

Values are Slack reaction short names, not the emoji themselves. An empty string
withdraws the reaction for that state.

```json
{
  "channels": {
    "slack": {
      "accounts": {
        "<alias>": {
          "bot_token": "YOUR_BOT_TOKEN",
          "status_reactions": true,
          "reaction_emojis": {
            "accepted": "hourglass_flowing_sand",
            "running": "hourglass_flowing_sand",
            "done": "",
            "failed": "warning"
          }
        }
      }
    }
  }
}
```

The app needs the `reactions:write` scope. Without it the API answers
`missing_scope`, which is logged once and then disabled for that account.

## Backward compatibility

- Both keys are optional and default to the pre-change behavior. With
  `status_reactions` false (the default), `setTaskReaction` returns before
  building a plan or touching the network, so existing Slack deployments are
  unaffected.
- The new vtable field carries a default (`&defaultSetTaskReaction`), so no
  existing channel implementation has to change.
- Telegram's vtable is untouched and `telegram.TaskReaction` still names the same
  enum, so Telegram behavior and its tests are unchanged.
- No config migration is needed.

## Rollback

The change is one commit. `git revert <sha>` restores the previous behavior;
because both keys are optional and default to off, nothing has to be undone in a
config file.

## Security impact

- The only new outbound requests are `reactions.add` and `reactions.remove` on
  the Slack Web API. Both require `reactions:write` and nothing else; no other
  scope, endpoint, file, or shell surface is added. The scope is only exercised
  when `status_reactions` is explicitly enabled.
- The request body is built with the existing `appendJsonStringW` escaper, so the
  channel id, timestamp, and reaction name are JSON-escaped rather than
  interpolated.
- No secret is logged. The failure path logs the endpoint name, the API error
  code, and the account alias. The bot token is not included.
- The reaction target comes from the inbound message's own channel and timestamp,
  so no new destination is derived from user input. `slackChannelIdOf` drops the
  thread suffix because Slack keys reactions by channel.

## Validation

Required by CONTRIBUTING.md and AGENTS.md for a code change:

```sh
zig build test --summary all   # 0 failures, 0 leaks
zig fmt --check src/           # .githooks/pre-commit
```

`zig build test --summary all` also runs from `.githooks/pre-push`. The pinned
toolchain is Zig 0.16.0 exactly.

Both commands were run on the PR head (`ea88ef3e`) with the pinned Zig 0.16.0
toolchain in a container:

```sh
$ zig fmt --check src/
(no output)

$ zig build test --summary all
Build Summary: 13/13 steps succeeded; 7501/7515 tests passed (14 skipped)
```

No test failed and no leak was reported; the 14 skipped tests are pre-existing
skips. CI is green on all three platforms for
[run 38655381046](https://github.com/nullclaw/nullclaw/actions/runs/38655381046):
`zig / linux-x86_64`, `zig / macos-aarch64`, and `zig / windows-x86_64` all
succeeded.

What the branch does cover without a network:

- `src/channels/slack.zig` adds 6 tests: the default transition table including
  the explicit removals, the shared-name case (0 removals on the `running`
  transition), the all-empty no-op case, the target parser, the inert path when
  `status_reactions` is off, and the vtable wiring. `callSlackApi` is stubbed
  under `builtin.is_test`, so none of these tests perform network I/O.
- `src/config.zig` adds 2 tests: defaults when the keys are absent, and an
  explicit config, both with the allocations freed.
- The existing `Channel message operations default to not supported` test in
  `src/channels/root.zig` gains an assertion that `setTaskReaction` returns
  `error.NotSupported` on the default vtable.

Manual check for a reviewer with a Slack app that has `reactions:write`: enable
`status_reactions`, send a message that triggers a turn, and watch the reaction
move through the configured names and disappear when `done` is set to an empty
string. That path is not covered by the automated tests.

## Notes

- Only the message that triggered the turn is reacted to. The agent's own reply is
  not, and no reaction is placed on a parent message.
- Reaction names are passed through to the API as configured. An unknown name
  comes back as an API error code, which `callSlackApi` logs; it does not affect
  the turn and does not disable reactions.
- Telegram still runs its own polling-loop lifecycle. A later change could point
  Telegram's vtable at the shared hook and delete the duplicate, but that is a
  separate concern and is not attempted here.

prs.title: feat(config): add agent.reasoning_mode default
prs.body:
> Tracking: #1066. This overlaps maintainer PR #1050 on the config key; see the comment below for how the two could be combined.

# feat(config): add agent.reasoning_mode default

- Branch: `feat/configurable-reasoning-default`
- Scope: one concern, a configurable default for the `/reasoning` display mode
- Risk tier (AGENTS.md §5): high, config schema. Change is additive only, no security, runtime, or gateway boundary is touched.
- Breaking change: no

## Summary

Adds the optional `agent.reasoning_mode` key (`off` | `on` | `stream`, default `off`) to the `agent` config section. It sets the reasoning display mode applied to newly created sessions, and it becomes the value `/restart` and `/debug reset` restore instead of the hard-coded `off`.

Diffstat (8 files, 182 insertions, 14 deletions):

```text
 docs/en/configuration.md | 18 ++++++++++
 docs/zh/configuration.md | 18 ++++++++++
 src/agent/commands.zig   |  2 +-
 src/agent/root.zig       | 49 +++++++++++++++++++--------
 src/config.zig           | 72 ++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++
 src/config_mutator.zig   |  1 +
 src/config_parse.zig     |  5 +++
 src/config_types.zig     | 31 +++++++++++++++++
 8 files changed, 182 insertions(+), 14 deletions(-)
```

## What changed

### `src/config_types.zig` (+31)

- New `pub const ReasoningMode` enum with variants `off`, `on`, `stream`, plus `toSlice()` and a case-insensitive `fromSlice()`.
- New field `AgentConfig.reasoning_mode: ReasoningMode = .off`.
- The enum is declared in the config layer so a parsed value can be assigned to the runtime field with no conversion step.

### `src/config_parse.zig` (+5)

- `parseJson` reads `agent.reasoning_mode`. A non-string value or an unrecognized string returns `error.InvalidReasoningMode`, so a typo fails loudly instead of silently falling back to `off`.

### `src/config.zig` (+72)

- `Config.save()` emits `reasoning_mode` inside the pretty-printed `agent` section, so a saved config round-trips through `parseJson`.
- New tests: `parse agent.reasoning_mode`, `agent.reasoning_mode defaults to off`, `agent.reasoning_mode rejects invalid values`, `Config.save preserves agent.reasoning_mode`.

### `src/config_mutator.zig` (+1)

- `pathRequiresRestart` returns true for `agent.reasoning_mode`, alongside the existing `agent.default_queue_mode` entry. This matches the documented behavior that new sessions pick the value up after a restart.

### `src/agent/root.zig` (+36 / -13)

- Deletes the private `ReasoningMode` enum and aliases `config_types.ReasoningMode`, removing the conversion that would otherwise be needed when applying the configured value.
- New field `default_reasoning_mode: ReasoningMode = .off`, documented as the value restored by `/restart` and `/debug reset`.
- `Agent.fromConfig` sets both `reasoning_mode` and `default_reasoning_mode` from `cfg.agent.reasoning_mode`.
- New test `Agent.fromConfig applies agent.reasoning_mode and resets to it` covers the configured default, a per-session `/reasoning on` override, and the reset path, and carries a `Regression:` comment citing the idle-eviction problem.

### `src/agent/commands.zig` (+1 / -1)

- `resetRuntimeCommandState` sets `self.reasoning_mode = self.default_reasoning_mode` instead of `.off`. This is the shared code path behind `/restart` and `/debug reset`, so one change fixes both commands.

### `docs/en/configuration.md` (+18) and `docs/zh/configuration.md` (+18)

- New `agent.reasoning_mode` section in both languages, placed next to the other `agent.*` keys. CONTRIBUTING requires syncing English and Chinese pages when both audiences are affected, and this is a user-facing config key, so both pages are updated in this PR to satisfy that requirement.

## Why it changed

`reasoning_mode` always started at `off`, and `resetRuntimeCommandState` hard-coded `.off` for `/restart` and `/debug reset`. Sessions are evicted after `agent.session_idle_timeout_secs`, so anyone who wants reasoning visible had to re-run `/reasoning on` after every idle eviction.

The display mode is a preference, not per-session state, so it belongs in the `agent` config section. `agent.default_queue_mode` already solves the same class of problem for the queue mode, so this follows an existing pattern rather than introducing a new one. This also gives the new key a concrete caller in `Agent.fromConfig` and `resetRuntimeCommandState`, as required by AGENTS.md §3.2.

`/reasoning <mode>` still overrides the mode for the current session. The config key only changes what a new or reset session starts from.

## Validation

Run locally on the PR head (`76beefede3a1f4b0e3c53680948476b931b14357`) with Zig 0.16.0:

```text
zig fmt --check src/            # clean, no output
zig build test --summary all    # Build Summary: 13/13 steps succeeded; 7498/7512 tests passed (14 skipped)
```

The test run completed with 0 failures and 0 leaks; the 14 skipped tests are the platform-gated ones. CI on the same commit is green on all three platforms: https://github.com/nullclaw/nullclaw/actions/runs/38655334578 (linux-x86_64, macos-aarch64, windows-x86_64).

Required for code changes (CONTRIBUTING, AGENTS.md §8), with Zig 0.16.0:

```bash
zig build test --summary all      # must be 0 failures and 0 leaks
zig fmt --check src/              # the same check .githooks/pre-commit runs
```

Optional release check, since the change touches config and agent paths:

```bash
zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseSmall
```

Test coverage added by this PR (AGENTS.md §8.1), 5 tests total:

- `src/config.zig`: `parse agent.reasoning_mode`, `agent.reasoning_mode defaults to off`, `agent.reasoning_mode rejects invalid values`, `Config.save preserves agent.reasoning_mode`
- `src/agent/root.zig`: `Agent.fromConfig applies agent.reasoning_mode and resets to it`

## Config surface

- Key: `agent.reasoning_mode`
- Type: string enum, one of `off`, `on`, `stream` (case-insensitive)
- Default: `off`
- Optional: yes. A config that does not set the key behaves exactly as it does today.

```json
{
  "agent": {
    "reasoning_mode": "stream"
  }
}
```

- `off` hides reasoning content, `on` prints a `Reasoning:` quote block above the final reply, `stream` prints reasoning live while the model produces it.
- `/reasoning <off|on|stream>` overrides the mode for the current session only.
- Changes apply to sessions created after a restart. `config_mutator.pathRequiresRestart` reports this for `nullclaw config set`.

## Risks and follow-up work

- Risk: a config typo now fails config loading instead of being ignored. This is intentional (AGENTS.md §3.4 fail fast) and matches how `agent.default_queue_mode` already behaves.
- Risk: `ReasoningMode` moves from `src/agent/root.zig` to `src/config_types.zig`. Both are internal to the module; no public API is exported and no caller outside these files references the type.
- Follow-up, deliberately not in this PR to keep it single-concern: `resetRuntimeCommandState` also resets `verbose_level` and `usage_mode` to fixed values, which could get the same configurable-default treatment.

## Breaking change

No. The key is optional and defaults to `off`, which is the pre-change behavior for both the initial mode and the reset path. No existing key changes meaning, no CLI flag is removed, and no config file needs editing.

## Rollback

- `git revert` the commit, or
- set `agent.reasoning_mode` back to `off` (or remove the key) and restart. Sessions then behave exactly as they did before this change.

## Notes

- The reset path and the config default now read the same field, so there is a single source of truth for "what mode does a new session start in".
- `/reasoning` command parsing is unchanged. Only the initial value and the reset value moved.
- No new dependency and no new allocation on the hot path. The addition to `Agent` is one small enum field next to the existing `reasoning_mode`.
- No secrets, tokens, or personal data are included in the code, tests, docs, or this description.

prs.title: feat(telegram): opt-in rich messages via sendRichMessage
prs.body:
Tracked in #1066.

## Summary

Telegram's Bot API 10.1 added Rich Messages: `sendRichMessage` and the `rich_message` parameter on `editMessageText` accept GFM Markdown and render headings, tables, task lists, footnotes, `==mark==`, `||spoiler||` and `$math$` natively. This adds an opt-in, per-account flag that uses that path for single-message replies and in-place edits.

- `channels.telegram.accounts.<id>.rich_messages` (bool, default `false`) enables the rich path for that account. `TelegramChannel.initFromConfig` copies it into `rich_messages_enabled`.
- When enabled, the send path (`sendSplitTextWithMarkdownFallbackWithMarkup`) sends one `sendRichMessage`, and the edit path (`editMessageWithMarkdownFallback`) sends one `editMessageText` with `rich_message`, instead of the HTML/plain split path.
- The rich path is used only when the escaped reply fits in a single rich message (at most 32768 Unicode codepoints, measured after escaping). A longer reply, an escaping failure, or any rich API error falls back directly to the legacy split/HTML path. A rich-related Telegram error (`can't parse`, `message is too long`, `Not Found`, ...) triggers the fallback; a non-rich error (401, 403, 429, chat not found, message not modified, ...) is surfaced once and not retried twice (`telegram_api.responseIsRichRelatedError`).
- `escapeRichMarkdown` passes the model's own GFM through, escaping only `<` outside code spans, fenced blocks and indented code, and degrades GFM tables wider than 20 columns to a code block (the rich API caps tables at 20 columns).
- When enabled, the system prompt tells the model that this Telegram chat renders rich Markdown. The flag is carried on `ConversationContext.rich_formatting` so it is set only for the account's turns.

Off by default. Some current Desktop, Web and Android clients and third-party clients render accepted rich messages as an unsupported placeholder, so this stays opt-in. With the flag off the send and edit paths are unchanged (the same legacy functions are called); a regression test pins the legacy chunking at 4096 and 5000 characters.

### Bot API changelog

- Bot API 10.1 (June 11, 2026) added Rich Messages: the `sendRichMessage` method, `sendRichMessageDraft`, the `rich_message` parameter on `editMessageText`, and the `RichMessage`/`InputRichMessage` classes.
- Bot API 10.3 (August 24, 2026) extended them with rich-message buttons, expandable block quotations and documents, and `is_compact` on `RichBlockTable`.
- The documented limits this change relies on: up to 32768 UTF-8 characters and up to 20 columns in a table.

This uses only the 10.1 surface (`sendRichMessage`, `editMessageText` + `rich_message`) with the `markdown` form, so it works on any Bot API server that has 10.1.

### OpenClaw reference

OpenClaw has the same opt-in and the same fallback shape:

- `extensions/telegram/src/rich-messages-config.ts` resolves `richMessages` per account (`resolveTelegramRichMessages`) and turns it off for caller-authored HTML sends.
- `extensions/telegram/src/rich-plain-fallback.ts` degrades a rich send to plain text on `RICH_MESSAGE_*_INVALID`, oversized payloads and the structural limits, including `TABLE_COLS_TOO_MANY` (over 20 table columns).
- `docs/channels/telegram/rich-messages.md` documents the config key, the default-off client-compatibility rationale, the 20-column table fallback and the automatic long-message split.

- [rich-messages.md](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/fead50a35107ed73cbb1f34b93c21716a0583f98/docs/channels/telegram/rich-messages.md)
- [rich-messages-config.ts](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/fead50a35107ed73cbb1f34b93c21716a0583f98/extensions/telegram/src/rich-messages-config.ts)
- [rich-plain-fallback.ts](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/fead50a35107ed73cbb1f34b93c21716a0583f98/extensions/telegram/src/rich-plain-fallback.ts)

One difference: OpenClaw parses Markdown into typed Bot API rich blocks and keeps model text away from the rich-Markdown sigils. This change sends the model's GFM text directly to the `rich_message.markdown` field and escapes only `<`, which is why the escaping caveat below is documented.

### Related upstream work

Prior-art search (open and closed PRs, issues, all open PR titles) found no existing PR or issue for Telegram rich messages (`sendRichMessage` / `rich_message` / `rich_messages` / GFM). The nearest earlier channel work is #596 (abstract an `OutboundPayload` port and add `sendRich` for DingTalk and Lark Card 2.0) and #458 (route structured assistant replies through the rich channel port); both are channel-port abstractions, not the Telegram rich-message API. #1062 (render live drafts with HTML parse mode) is related but independent: it changes how the live draft body is rendered, this changes the final send and edit path, and they touch different hunks of `src/channels/telegram.zig`.

## Validation

Zig 0.16.0, on this branch (based on `main` at 5f1cade0):

```text
$ zig fmt --check src/
$ zig build test --summary all
Build Summary: 13/13 steps succeeded; 7520/7534 tests passed (14 skipped)
$ zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseSmall
```

Tests added (in `src/channels/telegram.zig`, `src/channels/telegram_api.zig`, `src/agent/prompt.zig`, `src/config.zig`):

- `escapeRichMarkdown` passes `==mark==`, `||spoiler||`, `$math$` and currency through, escapes raw `<` to `\<`, does not double an existing `\<`, preserves GFM structure, and leaves inline code spans, fenced blocks and indented code blocks verbatim.
- Table handling: 20 columns stay inline, 21+ columns (with or without a leading pipe) are wrapped in a code fence, and pipes inside inline code are not counted as columns.
- `sendRichMessage` / `editMessageText` bodies carry `rich_message.markdown` (JSON-encoded), keep `reply_parameters` and `reply_markup`, and omit `parse_mode` / `text`.
- `responseIsRichRelatedError` classifies rich-format errors as fallback-worthy and 401/403/429/`chat not found`/`message not modified` as not.
- `initFromConfig` enables the rich path only when `rich_messages` is true; the fallback warning is logged once per account.
- `buildConversationContext` preserves `rich_formatting` and the prompt mentions rich Markdown only when it is set.
- Legacy chunking is unchanged with rich messages off (a 4000-char reply is one message; 4096 is one; 5000 splits at 4096).

Verified live on Telegram by the author: with `rich_messages` enabled, a reply containing a heading, a table, a task list, `==mark==`, `||spoiler||` and `$math$` renders natively; the same reply with the flag off renders through the existing HTML path.

Trial-merged onto `main` + #971 (native tool calls while streaming): merges cleanly, no conflicts, and both checks pass:

```text
$ zig fmt --check src/
$ zig build test --summary all
Build Summary: 13/13 steps succeeded; 7535/7549 tests passed (14 skipped)
```

## Notes

- Escaping caveat. Rich Markdown accepts the model's own GFM, so `==`, `||`, `$math$` and code are passed through unescaped; escaping them would make the advertised features unreachable. The only escape the Bot API documents is `\#hashtag`, and it states Rich Markdown "can contain arbitrary HTML". `\<` is therefore an assumption taken from GFM/CommonMark, where any ASCII punctuation may be backslash-escaped; it keeps a raw `<` in model output from being parsed as an HTML tag. If a client does not honour `\<`, a stray raw tag renders as a literal tag (cosmetic, and only reachable when the model emits raw HTML despite the prompt telling it not to).
- Based on plain `main`; #971 is not included. #971 is in the provider/SSE layer, this is in the Telegram channel layer, so they do not overlap. Trial-merging this branch onto `main` + #971 produces no conflicts and the suite passes (result above).
- Independent of #1062 (render live drafts with HTML parse mode). #1062 changes the live draft body; this changes the final send and edit path. They touch different hunks of `src/channels/telegram.zig` and can land in either order. They are not combined here.
- Files changed: `src/channels/telegram.zig`, `src/channels/telegram_api.zig`, `src/config_types.zig`, `src/config.zig`, `src/agent/prompt.zig`, `src/channel_loop.zig`, `docs/en/configuration.md`, `docs/zh/configuration.md`. No change to the shared splitter or limits; the rich-off path is byte-identical to upstream.
